conference.title: Statement from the Pac-12 Conference
conference.summary: On Friday, Oct. 30, 2026, the Pac-12 Conference issued the following public statement regarding discriminatory behavior at Pac-12 home venues this season. On Saturday, Oct. 24, the conference was notified of religiously discriminatory conduct directed at Utah State student-athletes and fans during Texas State’s home football game. Similar conduct has occurred at games across college football this season, including one other of our own member institutions. There is no place for such behavior in any venue, nor should it be tolerated. The league has reviewed the preventive measures in place at both instances at Pac-12 venues this season, and will be working with its Board of Directors to strengthen fan conduct standards and accountability, both to prevent this behavior at our own games and to better protect our student-athletes and fans across any sporting events. ?

Following an embarrassing 31-14 loss at Utah State, Jim Mora unleashed a fiery postgame tirade unlike anything we've heard from a CSU head coach in years. Gonzaga.title: No. 15 Gonzaga holds narrow lead against Purdue in season opener in Las Vegas | Live updates
Gonzaga.summary:
Follow along with this thread for updates throughout the game.

Zag lead hits double digits

2nd half, 11:57 – Gonzaga 56, Purdue 48 – Izan Almansa, the former pro from Spain, continues to impress in his GU debut.

The 6-10 forward fought through contact and converted a layup, drawing a foul and finishing the three-point play to put GU up 56-46 before the Boilermakers answered with another jump hook from 7-footer Daniel Jacobsen. 

Almansa now has 11 points of 4 of 6 shooting, joining two other Zags in double figures.

Quick burst extends GU lead

2nd half, 14:50 – Gonzaga 51, Purdue 42: In a blink the Zags opened up a game-high nine-point lead.

Izan Almansa hit a pair of free throws, then Purdue answered with a jumper before Almansa’s second jam of the game. Xaivian Lee rebounded a Boilermaker miss on the other end, then drilled a stepback 3-pointer, igniting the Zag bench and the large contingent of GU supporters in Vegas.

The two Zag newcomers are looking like very solid additions.

Purdue big man creates matchup problems

2nd half, 15:59 – Gonzaga 44, Purdue 40: Purdue’s offense is revolving around 7-footer Daniel Jacobsen, who put in three straight shots from close range. But Jacobsen just went to the bench with his third foul, which could be a major development.

The Zags haven’t scored a field goal over the last 2:40, but they’re moving the ball inside and drawing fouls, and preserving their lead from the line. Lee is into double figures in his Zag debut after he drove into the paint and drew a goaltend.

Zags take lead into break

Halftime – Gonzaga 36, Purdue 33: An energetic, highly entertaining first half in the season opener ended with the Zags holding a narrow lead after Davis Fogle knocked down a difficult reverse layup in traffic in the final minute.

Neither team led by more than six points and the first half featured nine lead changes. Purdue hit 1 of its last 8 field goals in the half and committed three turnovers over the final three minutes.

The Zags’ 3-point shooting was the difference. They went 5 of 8 compared to Purdue’s 4-for-13 mark from beyond the arc. GU is shooting 15 of 28 (54%) overall and the Boilermakers are 14 of 31 (45%) from the floor. Rebounding and turnovers are about even.

Fogle leads all players with 11 points (5 of 10). Lee has six points on a pair of 3s. Huff has been held to five points on 2 of 5. Pacing Purdue is 7-4 center Daniel Jacobsen (eight points).

GU’s 3-point shooting impresses

1st half, 1:50 – Gonzaga 34, Purdue 33: Outside shooting was an issue for the Zags last year. That doesn’t seem to be the case with this team.

GU is 5 of 8 from 3-point range. Transfer point guard Xaivian Lee is 2 of 2 from deep. He just answered a 3 from Purdue’s Pierce with a contested triple.

The Boilermakers used a 7-0 spurt to take the lead before Lee’s first 3 calmed things down for GU. Transfer guard Javon Bennett, Fogle and Diop also have hit 3s.

The teams are both playing with pace and making extra passes. It’s been a pretty fluid half, despite all the newness on the court for both sides.

Fogle heats up, Zags take lead

1st half, 7:51 – Gonzaga 26, Purdue 23 – Sophomore standout Davis Fogle scored five quick points, including a 3, for the Zags to put them up by a game-high six points, but the Boilermakers halted the mini run. Purdue hit three straight shots.

Huff showed off his fancy footwork to answer a basket from his high school teammate, Purdue’s Caden Pierce.

The Zags are shooting 12 of 19 (63%) from the field. They already have nine assists.

Teams trading buckets in entertaining start

1st half, 11:43 – Gonzaga 16, Purdue 14: Both teams are finding a rhythm offensively, capitalizing on nice feeds to post players. Both teams are shooting 7 of 13 from the field after a fast-paced, back-and-forth stretch. Diop had a nice assist to Braden Huff for a layup, and GU newcomer Izan Almansa, a former Spanish pro, converted on a perfect dish from Huff before jamming a two-handed dunk. But the Boilermakers have answered every basket.

Post players start fast

1st half, 15:54, Gonzaga 6, Purdue 6: Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop, a 7-1 center, knocked down his first bucket in a Zags uniform. And unexpectedly, it wasn’t from close range. Diop drained a 3-pointer for GU’s first basket of the season.

But Purdue big man Daniel Jacobsen answered with back-to-back makes in the paint. Diop responded with a block before a rejection from the 7-4 Jacobsen on a Davis Fogle attempt. The game is tied 6-6 at a timeout at the 15:54 mark. The teams have combined to shoot 5 of 12 in the early goings.

GU’s new-look lineup

The Zags are rolling with three transfers and two returners in their starting lineup.

Their backcourt includes Florida transfer Xaivian Lee, who gained a fifth year of eligibility when a California court granted a temporary restraining order against the NCAA, and Houston transfer Isiah Harwell. Sophomore returner Davis Fogle is starting at wing while senior standout Braden Huff and Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop will occupy the post spots.

Zags looking for first win against Purdue

The college hoops heavyweights have matched up five times before, and Purdue has won them all.

The Boilermakers beat the visiting Zags 83-68 in the teams’ first meeting in November 1998. GU got a rematch the following season in the NCAA Tournament, but the 10th-seeded Zags fell to sixth-seeded Purdue 75-66 in the Sweet 16.

The teams didn’t meet again for over two decades. They squared off in November 2022 at the Phil Knight Legacy tournament in Portland, and 24th-ranked Purdue knocked off No. 6 Gonzaga 84-66 to advance to the tourney championship game.

The next season, the second-ranked Boilermakers, led by star big man Zach Edey, beat GU 73-63 in a Maui Invitational quarterfinal game in November. The most recent meeting came during the same season, in the Sweet 16 of the 2024 NCAA Tournament, where top-seeded Purdue, again led by Edey, topped fifth-seeded Gonzaga 80-68.

“I’ve been haunted by Zach Edey,” GU coach Mark Few said Monday during a pregame interview on TNT. “I think he’s still in Memphis (with the NBA’s Grizzlies).”

Few talks matchup in pregame interview

The Zags’ Hall of Fame coach discussed his team’s roster rebuild and its big season-opening matchup with the Boilermakers on TNT before the game.

“We’re trying our best,” Few said of GU’s roster makeover. “It’s been challenging, but it’s been fun. It’s been a great group to work with, a lot of positive energy and a bunch of different skill sets. It’s actually been fun.”

“The biggest challenge,” Few said, is making sure the new-look team “plays to our strengths” and finds situational matchups. To earn their first-ever win over Purdue, the Bulldogs need to win a “battle of toughness,” Few said.

”(The Boilermakers) are always so tough and so disciplined and well-coached. You have to beat them. They’re not going to beat themselves.”

Pregame

The time for roster building, transfers, eligibility appeals and speculation is finally behind the Gonzaga men’s basketball team.

Now it’s time to actually play basketball.

The No. 15 Zags tip off their season against Purdue in the Hall of Fame Series tonight at 4:30 p.m. from T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas. The game will be broadcast on TNT.

It’s a matchup that features two of the game’s top coaches in recent Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame inductee Mark Few and Matt Painter, who has led the Boilermakers to 11 straight NCAA Tournaments and was national runner-up in 2024.

Gonzaga will feature a formidable frontcourt with senior power forward Braden Huff back from injury, Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop at center and sophomore Davis Fogle coming off the wing.

The Zags will hope that trio, aided by a new-look backcourt assembled after an offseason of upheaval, will amount to a winning formula. The Zags are 4½-point favorites according to vegasinsider.com.

The Boilermakers are turning the page after an illustrious four-year career from point guard Braden Smith, who graduated from the program as the NCAA career assists leader. Look for 7-foot-4 center Daniel Jacobsen to make a big impact inside.

Gonzaga.title: Text chat has stoked friendly fire between Braden Huff, Xaivian Lee, Caden Pierce ahead of Gonzaga-Purdue opener
Gonzaga.summary:
Former Glenbard West High School teammates Braden Huff and Caden Pierce had already spent months bantering over text messages about the impending matchup between their Gonzaga and Purdue teams.

It was a fair fight until Aug. 26, when one of Pierce’s ex-teammates at Princeton became Huff’s newest teammate at Gonzaga. Xaivian Lee was thrown into the crosshairs when the point guard committed to Gonzaga, joining Mark Few’s roster as a late 5-in-5 addition. Huff didn’t wait long to create a group text message chat for the three players uniquely connected through different stages of their basketball journeys.

“Right when I committed, they threw me in a group chat,” Lee said. “First thing we talked about was this game. I obviously didn’t know if I was for sure going to be good then, but it’s looking like I’ll be good for that one at least.”

Huff’s relationship with Pierce goes back longer, but recency might give Lee a better idea of what to expect from the Purdue forward when he takes the floor for Matt Painter’s team Monday afternoon at T-Mobile Arena.

Lee and Pierce overlapped for three seasons at Princeton, playing in 91 games for teams that combined to go 91-25 between 2022-25. Pierce was the Ivy League Freshman of the Year in 2022-23 and Player of the Year in 2023-24. Lee came on strong toward the end of his tenure with the Tigers, earning All-Ivy League First Team honors in 2024-25 while averaging 16.9 points, 6.1 rebounds and 5.5 assists.

“Shoot, I might know (Pierce) better than Braden,” Lee joked. “He’s known him longer, but I’ve known him in college. It’s pretty special honestly. But we’ve just got to keep him off the glass. He’s a very talented rebounder and he’s in the right spots, so we’ve got to make sure we get a body on him and obviously pay attention to the scout and know what they’re doing on offense. But really for him, just keeping him off the glass I think.”

There’s a good chance Huff would’ve offered many of the same scouting tips on Pierce.

The Glen Elyn, Illinois , natives have known each other since fifth grade, playing on youth travel teams, the AAU Illinois Wolves and, most recently, the 2021-22 Glenbard West High squad that finished with a 37-1 record and captured the 2022 Illinois High School Association Class 4A title.

After Pierce’s junior season, the 6-foot-7 forward spent a year away from competition to focus on getting an undergraduate economic degree from Princeton. In the meantime, he’d browse transfer options for his final year of basketball eligibility. Gonzaga emerged as one of Pierce’s final five choices – along with Purdue, Duke, UConn and Louisville – and Huff hosted his longtime pal during a Jan. 2 recruiting visit to Spokane.

“That’s my guy,” Huff said. “I’ve known him since elementary school, played since I think fifth grade, we’ve been on a team together. We talked a little bit of trash, tried to get him to come here originally and that fell through. I’m excited for the matchup, I know Xaivian’s got some history too with him at Princeton so it’s going to be a lot of fun to see him and his family after the game.”

Pierce ultimately chose Purdue and renowned coach Matt Painter. Purdue’s campus in West Lafayette, Indiana, is also located just 70 miles northwest of Indianapolis, where Caden’s older brother Alec is a standout wide receiver for the NFL’s Colts.

“I really think (Braden) didn’t want to get too involved because he wanted Caden to make the best decision for him, right?” Huff’s father, Alec, said. “But yeah, I think it obviously would’ve been pretty cool. I think Caden’s super happy where he is, I think it’s a good spot for him but I think it’s going to be a really interesting dynamic when the three of those guys take the court together.”

The two players and their families have stayed close through the years. The Huffs joined the Pierces for one of Alec’s NFL games at Lucas Oil Stadium and traveled to Chapel Hill, North Carolina , in 2019-20 to watch oldest brother Justin Pierce play basketball at North Carolina. Last year, the Pierces returned the favor, accompanying the Huffs to watch Braden and Gonzaga play UCLA at Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle – a trip Alec Huff said was unrelated to Caden’s ongoing recruiting process.

“They’re good buds,” Alec Huff said. “They were in the same social circle, same group of friends in middle school and high school.”

Go figure, Huff and Pierce are also represented by the same agency, Chicago-based Priority Sports. It’s not uncommon for them to train together when both are home in Illinois during the offseason.

The Gonzaga-Purdue matchup was a topic of conversation during workouts this summer and the friendly banter only continued when Lee entered the fold in August. Below Lee’s commitment graphic on Instagram, Pierce commented “what is life.” Lee replied, “see ya in vegas.”

The fifth-year Florida transfer wasn’t sure if he’d be eligible for Monday’s opener, but a recent 5-in-5 ruling in California meant he’d be in the clear for the time being. Since August, Pierce has been taking barbs from both Gonzaga players in the group chat – something that probably feels a little bit like trying to defend a 2-on-1 fastbreak in transition.

“Every time we talk, I tell him we’re going to win,” Lee said. “He’s more humble than I am, so he says nothing really back to me. We definitely have some banter about it.”

Pierce and Lee have particularly fond memories of the 2022-23 season at Princeton, when the 15th-seeded Tigers stunned former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd and second-seeded Arizona in the first round of the NCAA Tournament.

“We were both freshmen on that team,” Lee recalled. “He was rookie of the year, he had like 16 rebounds maybe against Missouri in the second round. We were on a really good team that year, then the next year we kind of both got to run the show a little bit and we were really good that season as well.”

Lee and Huff are both expected to be in Gonzaga’s starting lineup when the ball is tipped on Monday. Pierce, a versatile wing, is on track to do the same after starting in each of Purdue’s three exhibitions.

Huff ’s and Pierce’s community of Glen Ellyn should be well-represented in Vegas. Both families are planning to attend Monday’s game, as is Glenbard West coach Jason Opoka, who faces a win-win/lose-lose situation with former players on both teams.

Huff’s 1-0 record against former Glenbard teammates could be a good omen for Monday. In 2024, he scored 14 points off the bench to help Gonzaga cruise past Bobby Durkin and Davidson, 90-65, at the Battle 4 Atlantis.

“It’s going to be an interesting deal,” Alec said of Monday’s game. “I think that’s going to be an issue for a few people in our community, to be honest with you.”

Gonzaga.title: Years in the making: No. 15 Gonzaga ready to roll out new roster in high-profile opener against Purdue
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – Two years ago, in Las Vegas of all places, Matt Painter was asked if Purdue had ever explored the idea of a home-and-home, nonconference series with Gonzaga.

The setting and timing both felt appropriate for the question. Painter was helping out at USA Olympic Basketball Camp on UNLV’s campus, working specifically with the USA Select Team. Gonzaga’s Mark Few was roaming the same practice gym on a scorching summer day in Vegas, working his offseason assignment with the Paris-bound men’s Olympic team.

There had been three chance meetings between Gonzaga and Purdue programs over the previous 20 months – on Nov. 25, 2022, at the Phil Knight Legacy in Portland, on Nov. 20, 2023, at the Maui Invitational in Honolulu and most recently, March 29, 2024, in the Sweet 16 of the NCAA Tournament.

Two of the most respected programs in college basketball. Two of the most revered coaches in the game. Why wouldn’t they want to get something on the books?

“We’ve talked about it,” Painter said on July 8, 2024. “Not home-and-home, but we’ve talked about neutral site.”

Voila, here they are two years later, matching up in Monday’s 4:30 p.m. neutral-site opener at T-Mobile Arena, just a few-hundred steps from the Vegas Strip. It’s one of two men’s games that will be part of this year’s Hall of Fame Series. Longtime Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd and Arizona will cap the night with a 7 p.m. tipoff against former Pac-12 rival UCLA. Both games will air on TNT.

“Purdue’s one of the real great programs we have in college basketball right now, Matt’s a heckuva coach and they’re just going to be a tough out,” Few said. “They’re very execution-oriented on offense and run a myriad of really, really nice actions, usually off the ball. But they’re big, they’ve always had those bigs inside. They’re man-to-man defense and they’ll pick us up full court and try to make every basket hard.”

That was the evaluation Few offered before even watching film from Purdue’s exhibition slate, which included a 76-53 loss to UConn and dominant 92-62 and 87-55 wins over Purdue Fort Wayne and Ball State. Gonzaga’s coaching staff doesn’t necessarily have to know Purdue’s personnel to know how Painter will try to scheme things up Monday night.

That goes both ways, obviously. The Boilermakers suspect the Bulldogs will try to speed the game up, play through an All-American-caliber post on offense and control the offensive and defensive glass. Mostly correct, although Few is still slightly skeptical about what his group can do from a rebounding standpoint.

“Great in transition, good size,” Painter said of the Zags. “Obviously getting (Massamba) Diop from Arizona State, good shot-blocker, good length. Braden Huff is an all-conference player, can score inside and out, can drive the basketball. Xaivian Lee at Princeton, at Florida, a lot of experience, very, very fast.

“There’s a couple areas for us that’s going to be important no matter who we play, but we have to do a better job of keeping people out of transition and these guys are really good in transition. And that starts with taking care of the basketball, taking good shots, setting your defense.”

From a personnel standpoint, there’s almost zero carryover from the last Gonzaga-Purdue matchup in 2024. Other than Huff, who scored four points in nine minutes off the bench, nobody else from either roster is back. Huff and Purdue’s C.J. Cox are also the only returning starters for their respective teams.

Cox could be the focal point of Gonzaga’s defensive plan. He’s the top returning scorer at 8.5 points per game and paced the Boilermakers through their exhibition slate, averaging 15.3 points and accounting for one-third of Purdue’s total scoring production against UConn with 18 points.

“A great set of guards,” Few said. “They shoot it well, they shoot it freely, they’re difficult to prepare with all the myriad of sets and actions they have and kind of challenge you in every way. They’re one of those teams that keep you in front, you’ve got to make shots over the top of them and are just phenomenal on the glass. Just the offensive glass and the defensive glass.”

Transfer wing Caden Pierce is expected to start in a small-ball “4” role for Purdue. Gonzaga doesn’t need to do much homework on the 6-foot-7 senior because Few’s staff did plenty last season when the Bulldogs tried to land a transfer commitment from Pierce, bringing him to Spokane for an official visit in January. Pierce is Huff’s former high school teammate at Glenbard West in the Chicago area and played with Lee for three seasons at Princeton.

“They seem to be really clicking with their execution. Obviously, I think they probably were all there this summer and adding Caden Pierce is a really, really nice addition,” Few said. “Really athletic and hard driving, hard playing kind of swing forward.”

Gonzaga’s expected to go with a starting unit of Lee, Isiah Harwell, Davis Fogle, Huff and Diop, but Few’s bench rotation could change in the hours leading up to Monday’s opener. Chauncey Wiggins is currently ineligible, but a judge in McLennan County, Texas, is still reviewing a temporary restraining order for the transfer wing and other player plaintiffs in his 5-in-5 lawsuit. A verdict is expected Monday, which could potentially reverse Wiggins’ eligibility status before the 4:30 p.m. start time in Vegas.

Gonzaga.title: Sizing up Gonzaga's roster, Purdue opener | Zags Basketball Insiders Podcast
Gonzaga.summary:
We’re back.

Richard Fox and yours truly touched on the pertinent topics in the first Zags Insiders podcast of the season, including Gonzaga’s roster, schedule, season predictions and Monday’s opener vs. Purdue.

Fox, former Zag center and longtime Gonzaga television analyst alongside Greg Heister and Dan Dickau, also discussed KHQ/SWX no longer being in GU’s television lineup. Their last game was Wednesday’s exhibition win over Lewis-Clark State.

Find the podcast at spokesman.com/podcasts/zags-basketball-insiders/ or on YouTube on The Spokesman-Review’s channel. Here are a few excerpts, edited for space considerations.

End of an era

Fox: My understanding is the Pac-12 really pushed to have all of the games period and certainly Gonzaga’s games picked up by one of their three partners – CW, CBS Sports, USA Network – so it kind of squeezed us out. Maybe down the road, around the corner KHQ can get a few more games, but for now it looks like the run is over.

We had breakfast a couple days before the (LCSC exhibition), we do that every year, and I was telling the boys, we did 13 years on TV, for Greg it’s 25, but then I did radio for four or five with Tom Hudson. Certainly disappointed it’s over at least for now. It was obviously a very unique experience, a unique way to stay close to the program as a former player, obviously fabulous seats on a regular basis.

To be able to do it for that long was a pretty amazing run.

Meehan: Heister said something to the effect that it’s the end of an era, and that’s pretty accurate.

That was a great (broadcasting) team. You’ve been the conduit for a lot of fans that can’t get into the games. They relied on you guys and it was a great run.

Huff working with new bigs, guards

Meehan: His touch around the rim, terrific scorer inside, efficiency off the charts. There’s going to be a lot on his plate this year. Graham (Ike) is making starts with the Golden State Warriors as a two-way player.

I think (GU coaches) are going to tell him, “We love your scoring, we’ve got to have you get on the glass.” That’s one of the issues throughout the year : How are they going to rebound?

I’m curious to see how it works with newcomer Massamba Diop, transfer from Arizona State whose strengths are so different than Graham’s strengths, and if that changes the operating room in there.

Fox: He looks healthy, first and foremost, and he’s improved his physique since he’s been at Gonzaga. He’s not a super explosive guy, but he has that kind of a shot put (shot). It’s really difficult as a defender because it comes off so quick. Braden is going to be, if not the focal point, at least No. 2 after (Davis) Fogle when it comes to their offense.

In today’s day and age, you have to acclimate to the new guys on your roster. When I think about Ike and (Drew) Timme, they had a lot of consistency at the point guard spot. I think it’s safe to say we don’t have that (Andrew and Ryan Nembhard, Jalen Suggs) level on the perimeter.

We might see some growing pains as this collective figures out how to play together but also for a guy like Braden who is a receiver not an initiator typically. If he can stay healthy, he’s going to have an All-Pac-12 type of year.

Best guesses on GU-Purdue

Fox: Purdue, it almost feels like what Gonzaga was five years ago in that maybe the apex of everything is kind of behind them just because they had that run not just with Edey but even before and they got to the final and then now they’re not returning a whole lot. They’re very well coached, they’re going to be big, they’ve always valued interior size.

It feels like a handful of teams, the UConns of the world, Duke, they’re able to sustain some consistency, but even they’re adding three, four, five pieces every year. The first part of the season in a lot of ways to me, is look and see. It’s a weird place to be where you’re listening, hoping we have some sort of feel and I don’t. I think it’s worth admitting that.

Gonzaga has two guys back. When you look at Purdue, who the hell knows. You have to give it until mid-November, even that Players Era (in Las Vegas), everyone is going to have much better feel for what they have and how everything fits.

Meehan: This isn’t the Purdue we’re used to seeing with Zach Edey in the NBA, Trey Kaufman-Renn with Kansas, Braden Smith in the NBA, (no) Fletcher Loyer. They have some guys back from last year, Gicarri Harris is probably the best of the bunch, 7-4 center (Daniel) Jacobsen and Caden Pierce, his brother is a great receiver for the Indianapolis Colts and (Caden) played high school ball with Huff and won an Illinois state championship, so a couple of old friends going at it.

Not the Purdue team we’re used to seeing the last few years. They’re right on the border of being ranked. These are complete guesses, but I don’t think it’s a bad matchup.

Gonzaga.title: A behind-the-scenes look at how Gonzaga managed a chaotic, unprecedented offseason: 'The obstacle is the way'
Gonzaga.summary:
Even in the offseason, college basketball coaches are inundated with recruiting calls, player evaluations, high school camps, summer workouts and other tasks that characterize the nonstop, 24/7/365 profession. There’s not as much downtime as the average fan would think but it does exist, usually in small pockets.

On July 10, Gonzaga assistant Stephen Gentry used one such window to take his son, Gunnar, to a screening of “Monsters & Minions.” The animated comedy wouldn’t have been Gentry’s first selection from the catalogue of motion pictures, but it was more about the father-son bonding time not always guaranteed to a college basketball assistant in 2026.

Ninety minutes you can’t put a price on.

Ninety-ish, it turned out.

Midfilm, Gentry felt a buzz in his pocket. He ignored the initial phone call, but vibrations persisted. Subtly, Gentry slid the device out of his pocket and read the notification: “two missed calls from Mark Few.” Probably should go see what that’s about, he figured.

With Gunnar still locked in on “Monsters & Minions,” Gentry left the theater and stepped into a hallway. He dialed Few and immediately learned why his boss was desperate to reach him, and on a Friday no less.

There had been whispers, murmurs about Mario Saint-Supery’s potential exit from the program, but this was Gonzaga’s coach formally delivering the news that would shake an offseason unlike any the Bulldogs have had since they planted their flag on the national stage three decades ago. In mid-July, after completing offseason workouts in Spokane and sitting in on Domantas Sabonis’ jersey dedication ceremony just 24 hours earlier, Gonzaga’s starting point guard was leaving to play for Spanish ACB club Valencia. The search to replace him might as well have started yesterday.

“I should’ve taken the phone call earlier,” Gentry said. “What an awful movie.”

Nearly 1,000 miles south, the longest-tenured member of Few’s staff – and the man in line to replace Gonzaga’s newly-minted Hall of Famer when he steps down – was handling one of those aforementioned offseason tasks. It was Friday morning and Brian Michaelson was roaming the Las Vegas Convention Center on a 110-degree day in Sin City, skipping from one court to the next inside the oversized conference hall-turned-bustling basketball venue. Gonzaga point guard commit Dooney Johnson and hundreds of high school prospects were competing at Nike EYBL AAU from July 8-13. Zags assistant Zach Norvell Jr. had been in the day prior for evaluations.

Friday’s slate of EYBL games wrapped before Michaelson got wind of Saint-Supery’s decision, but he was scheduled to return the next morning. It devolved into a chaotic Saturday – Michaelson juggling live evaluations at the convention center while simultaneously fielding phone calls from agents and high school/AAU coaches feeding him intel on replacement point guard options.

“I felt like that week, 10 days after that my phone was dead before lunch,” Michaelson said. “Especially I remember that week in Vegas, truly trying to charge my phone wherever I possibly could for like a minute or two so I could get a little more.”

Roughly a month later, Gentry was out at dinner with his wife, Leah, when he made the astute observation that Gonzaga’s frenetic offseason, with extreme twists and turns seemingly every week, could probably be distilled into a non-fiction novel.

“I think we got up to nine, where I could write a book about the last nine weeks where it was just every week, it was something,” Gentry said. “It was some sort of curveball with Jack (Kayil) and Mario. But I think in a lot of ways it really strengthened our staff and program. I think it just forced us to have our backs against the wall, forced us to communicate even more, to have even more of a plan.

“It’s the old adage, the obstacle is the way.”

• • •

Many believed Saint-Supery was on the precipice of a breakout sophomore season. The savvy Spaniard navigated bumps as a freshman, but those were anticipated from someone making the often-difficult basketball and lifestyle transition from Europe to the U.S. at the age of 19.

Saint-Supery’s closing stretch in 2025-26, coupled with the improvement those close to the program raved about through the early stages of the offseason, had coaches and teammates optimistic about what the point guard’s next act could look like.

Add in expectations around the player projected to be Saint-Supery’s running mate. Last November, Gonzaga signed prized German prospect and 19-year-old Alba Berlin pro Jack Kayil, a combo guard they figured would pair seamlessly with Saint-Supery in the starting lineup and handle on-ball responsibilities when the Spaniard was on the bench.

The running theory was Kayil would test NBA draft waters, attend the combine, collect feedback from NBA workouts and ultimately withdraw his name to play in college. Some mock drafts had Kayil pegged higher than others, but the consensus was he was a second-round prospect who still needed to fill out his frame and improve on the defensive end – two of the reasons a young prospect might choose to spend multiple years at Gonzaga.

Instead, the outcome with the lowest odds prevailed. Kayil, who reportedly got first-round NBA feedback, kept his name in the draft and went No. 39 overall (ninth pick of the second round) to the Houston Rockets, who traded him to the New York Knicks on draft night. Without a roster spot available, the reigning NBA champions declined to designate Kayil to the G League and instead stashed the guard in Europe. In August, he returned to Alba Berlin on a five-year contract.

“I think any college coach you talk to would say offseasons have been crazy and hectic … I think ours was probably exacerbated by the two guys we felt last spring when you and I would’ve talked were going to be our starting backcourt,” Michaelson said, characterizing their departures as “fairly late in the cycle,” and “definitely after the transfer portal, right?”

By the time Saint-Supery visited Gonzaga’s coaching offices on July 11 to meet with Gentry before returning to Spain – “a good chat, but also you can’t relish on it,” the sixth-year assistant said – Few’s staff had already started assembling names, with limited avenues available to them.

Bubbling with options in the spring, the transfer portal had become desolate by the middle of the summer. College basketball players have a three-week period from April 7-21 to submit their names in the portal, but top-end transfers often have a destination in mind before the window opens and make their choice by the end of the month. Case in point, Gonzaga’s top portal targets, guard Isiah Harwell (Houston) and center Massamba Diop (Arizona State), announced commitments on April 12 and 29, respectively.

There’s typically a few stragglers in May and early June, “but once you get past that, the options aren’t as plentiful and they’re not as straightforward,” Michaelson said.

And, mind you, this was July 11.

Right around the same time, a handful of college athletes, coaches and agents started kicking the tires on a new idea. The NCAA had recently introduced its 5-in-5 eligibility model. Five years to play as many seasons as you can squeeze into that firm window. Every class moving forward would benefit, but the NCAA took a hard stance on the high school class of 2022, asserting last year’s seniors would not be grandfathered in.

It rubbed some the wrong way, particularly in a climate where highly compensated college basketball players can earn more from revenue sharing and name, image and likeness in a single season than they might over five years in the G League or overseas. The high school classes of 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026 would capitalize from 5-in-5. The class of 2021 had a one-time waiver to play five seasons due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Why should 2022 be excluded?

“It’s really unfortunate they’re taking this stance,” Few said after Kraziness in the Kennel last month. “Classes before all these guys have gotten five, six, seven years. Now with our new rule, the classes after them. So I’m not sure why we’re sticking to targeting this one specific group.”

On July 9, one day before Saint-Supery’s defection, an all-conference point guard from Dayton named Javon Bennett was listed among the plaintiffs in the first of many lawsuits filed against the NCAA from class of 2022 graduates seeking relief. A judge ruled in favor of Bennett and others, granting an injunction that cleared the group to pursue a fifth year of eligibility.

With a new door opened and, in many ways, a new life extended to Gonzaga’s coaching staff, Few’s assistants started drafting lists. They’d assign players to “buckets,” determining which ones might be the best fit from a system and culture fit, but also which ones were most likely to make it through the legal process to suit up in 2026-27.

“We made a bunch of buckets of potential routes to go, potential avenues, and we knew nothing about the possible fifth-year bucket on that day one,” Michaelson said. “But it was a bucket that had to be discussed.”

Nobody on Few’s staff carries a Juris Doctor diploma in their back pocket, but Gonzaga’s coaches had to be somewhat versed in the legal terminology and ongoing court procedures to assess which players had the best chance of earning injunctions and temporary restraining orders. Semi-educated throws at the dartboard, more than anything else.

“We did have to try to – I’m far from an expert – become somewhat knowledgeable with what might happen, what could happen, different routes of that,” Michaelson said.

Michaelson continued to phone agents, AAU coaches, high school coaches and others to discuss options, ideally looking for players who could meet all six of his designated check marks, but at least four or five of them.

“You probably need to lean on the guy that has six check marks, not the guy that has one,” he said. “Hey, this guy’s got three. This (other) guy has three, but three different ones. Which three do we like better? The public’s seeing it play out now. It was really, really complicated and we’re still dealing with that on a day-to-day basis.”

The result? Gonzaga picked up commitments from two fifth-year point guards – Bennett and Florida’s Xaivian Lee – to fill the Saint-Supery/Kayil voids and one wing, Florida State’s Chauncey Wiggins, who’d bring elite outside shooting and size on the perimeter.

Three months later, there’s still not a firm answer as to whether all three, none of the three or some combination of the three will be eligible by the time Gonzaga opens its inaugural Pac-12 Conference schedule in January.

Recent court decisions allowed Lee, who has an injunction in California, and Bennett, who’s eligible through a stay from the Ohio Supreme Court, to suit up in Gonzaga’s preseason exhibitions while Wiggins was forced to sit out after a verdict in his Georgia lawsuit. The situation remains fluid with the effect unclear for Gonzaga. All three players could be one legal ruling from getting a green light to play the rest of the season, or from returning their Gonzaga uniforms and spending the next five months on the sideline.

Coaches, pundits and sports lawyers who’ve closely monitored the cases are bracing for a reality where certain fifth-year seniors are able to play in 2026-27 and others aren’t, solely based off how judges in different jurisdictions view the situation.

“Credit to them, I don’t know how they do it every day coming in, putting the work in, just keeping their heads down when some of them don’t even know if they’re going to be eligible,” sophomore forward Parker Jefferson said. “It’s a big credit to them, it’s a credit to the culture we have here.”

The next few chapters of the novel Gonzaga started writing in the offseason could be even more compelling than the first ones.

The Zags open the season Monday with a high-caliber showdown against Purdue in Las Vegas (4:30 p.m., TNT). Fans should probably buckle up for a season where Gonzaga’s starting unit changes night-to-night, week-to-week or month-to-month depending on how court rulings shake out. Bennett’s eligibility status, for example, has already flipped three times and could change again. Few and other coaches have pressed the NCAA to extend a blanket waiver to the class of 2022, but the regulatory body hasn’t budged since making its initial stance.

Gonzaga’s coaches are ready to leave a chaotic offseason in the rearview mirror, but they also insist they’re better off from the unique circumstances the last seven months lobbed their way – often multiple at a time and sometimes on the same day. Their roster may be better off, too.

“I think it really strengthened our staff and our program in a lot of ways and obviously we’re still navigating those curveballs and everything but I think golly, we upgraded at so many spots this offseason which is amazing to think with the curveballs and the situations we were in,” Gentry said. “But we feel like we totally upgraded at guard spots and actually came out of this with a better, stronger roster. We think not only the pieces individually upgraded, but I think the pieces fit together extremely well.”

It should make for a thrilling story, or novel, or movie. At least one Gentry will be happy to watch all the way through the final credits.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga men adjust on the fly after whirlwind offseason
Gonzaga.summary:
Anyone trying to get a feel for what Gonzaga’s strengths and weaknesses will be in 2026-27 may feel slightly better knowing the highly qualified coaches observing and analyzing practices inside the Volkar Center still aren’t totally sure, either.

“It’s wild that I can’t tell you on Oct. 21, because there’s still some uncertainty,” assistant Brian Michaelson said when asked about the group’s identity two weeks ago.

Will the Zags be an improved perimeter shooting team after posting the lowest 3-point percentages of the Mark Few era in consecutive seasons? Probably a safe bet, but it could depend on the eligibility of fifth-year transfer Chauncey Wiggins, a tall, smooth-shooting forward who made 157 3s during ACC stops at Clemson and Florida State.

“He’s far and away our best shooter and we could’ve used some 3s tonight,” Few said after watching the Zags miss 11 consecutive 3s and finish 6 of 28 during an exhibition loss to Arkansas. “I think that’s why I feel encouraged.”

Will the Zags have a stable of point guards that runs as deep as any in the country? Potentially, but it could require two more court decisions – one involving Florida transfer Xaivian Lee, another involving Dayton transfer Javon Bennett – swinging in their favor. If not, Frenchman Nathan De Sousa, the only point guard guaranteed to be eligible through March, will take on a significantly bigger load, raising more questions about one of the most important positions in Few’s system.

But while we’re on the topic of “what-ifs,” consider this one: What if the Zags only require marginal depth and role talent around a Big Four of Braden Huff, Davis Fogle, Massamba Diop and Isiah Harwell in order to sustain a top-15 ranking, capture a Pac-12 championship and march back to the Sweet 16 after second-round exits each of the last two years?

Most notably, Huff is back in the fold after missing the final two months of his junior season with a left knee injury. Early signs suggest there’s been no drop-off in the crafty forward’s conditioning or low-post game and he led all scorers with 19 points against Arkansas.

Huff will be paired next to Diop, the towering Arizona State transfer who chose Few’s program at Gonzaga over Rick Pitino’s at St. John’s in a high-stakes portal bidding war between Naismith Hall of Fame coaches. Diop isn’t nearly as refined around the basket as Huff’s previous running mate, Graham Ike, but he offers a level of rim protection the Zags haven’t had since Chet Holmgren and could thrive as a lob threat when opponents look to double Huff.

“Graham and B-Huff are both big guys, but obviously Massamba’s just 7-foot -plus, so to have legitimate size and strength at both those positions is something we’re really excited about, something we really wanted,” Michaelson said. “Then I do think their skill sets will complement each other. They’re both unselfish players, B-Huff is obviously a big-time, big-time scorer. Massamba’s ability to run the floor, Massamba’s ability to be a lob and shot-blocking threat. They can both drive the ball, they can both make an outside shot.

“You can post one and the other can be off the ball. You can ball -screen with one and the other can be off the ball, they can have a skill overlap that fits together.”

If Huff isn’t leading the Zags in scoring average at the end of the season, that honor will likely go to Fogle, an attack-minded wing who can hurt opponents at all three levels. Fogle averaged 10.9 points once he became a full-fledged member of GU’s rotation last season and opened a few more eyes with a blistering 30-point performance – in only 20 minutes of game action – at Kraziness in the Kennel. The slender 6-foot-7 sophomore worked to add more muscle this offseason and fine-tuned his 3-point shooting stroke – a change that was evident at Kraziness, when he connected on 6 of 7 shots from behind the arc.

“He’s got such an awesome love for the game, a high care factor, he’s super passionate about his craft that if he wants to be here extra, he wants to be in here,” assistant coach Stephen Gentry said. “It’s part of what makes him awesome and so great is his drive and love for the game of basketball and competing.”

The biggest X factor could be Harwell, a five-star high school prospect thought to be a NBA lottery pick candidate before injuries and inconsistent offensive play hindered his freshman year at Houston. Harwell has the potential to be Gonzaga’s most effective two-way player as a bigger two-guard who can manufacture his own shots on offense and simultaneously handle the top assignment at the other end of the floor.

After making 27.1% of his 3s at Houston, Harwell believes he’s rediscovered the 3-point accuracy that made him one of the nation’s top recruiting prospects a year ago. There’s already proof, too. Harwell went 5 of 7 from beyond the arc and finished 10 of 14 from the field in his first two public outings wearing a Gonzaga uniform (Kraziness and Arkansas).

“I feel like I lost a little bit of confidence in myself coming from Houston,” Harwell said. “Staying in the gym and working on it day and night with B-Mike and Snacks (assistant Zach Norvell Jr.) really helped me. Repetition and getting that confidence back that I was a good shooter.”

Gonzaga’s depth will be dictated by the ongoing, unpredictable 5-in-5 lawsuits. If eligible, Lee presumably slides into the starting point guard role, pushing De Sousa to the bench, where he could be joined by Wiggins and Bennett – veteran players with 2,533 career points and three NCAA Tournament appearances between them.

The bench unit will also feature Izan Almansa, an experienced Spanish forward who gives the Zags a rebounding presence they lack elsewhere in the frontcourt. Twenty-four hours after learning he was eligible, Almansa was an instant-impact player against Arkansas, scoring 12 points with six rebounds off the bench.

If the Zags get bad news on the eligibility front, they’ll either tighten up their rotation or turn to a younger group of reserve players. Freshmen wings Luca Foster and Juwan Ekanga showed flashes of potential during preseason scrimmages/exhibitions. Sophomore forward Parker Jefferson and freshman center Sam Funches will be GU’s emergency bigs, but won’t expect to see much time behind the trio of Huff, Diop and Almansa.

Gonzaga.title: Mark Few, Brian Michaelson reminisce on building Gonzaga's 2016-17 roster, magical season: "It was the perfect mix"
Gonzaga.summary:
Early in the 2016-17 college basketball season – Game 2, to be exact – No. 14 Gonzaga led by as many as 30 and hammered fellow West Coast power San Diego State 69-48.

The postgame was probably more interesting than the beatdown on the McCarthey Center court.

“Coach (Steve) Fisher told me right after the game, ‘You’re good enough to go to a Final Four,’ and I was, ‘C’mon coach, it’s our first real game,’ ” Gonzaga coach Mark Few recalled. “He was like, ‘No, no, no, you are.’ That guy knows, he’d been there (with Michigan) and he was a guy I looked up to. I’ve always remembered that.”

Fisher no doubt took notice of GU’s tall, talented and experienced roster that limited the Aztecs to 29% shooting, 24% on 3-pointers, won the glass, snagged 13 steals and swatted eight shots. Those would become seasonlong defensive traits as Gonzaga broke through to reach its first Final Four.

Even with GU enduring a rare subpar shooting performance (39%), the offensive balance was evident. Eventual leading scorer Nigel Williams-Goss had just 10 points, but Cal transfer Jordan Mathews delivered 17.

Super subs Zach Collins and Killian Tillie combined for 23 points and 18 boards to offset uncharacteristic quiet nights from Przemek Karnowski and Johnathan Williams. Those four would form one of the nation’s finest frontcourts.

Gonzaga’s impressive collection of players was five years in the making, from Few and then lead assistant coach Tommy Lloyd traveling to Poland to land the 7-foot-1 Karnowski to Mathews transferring in at the end of June – late in the 2016 recruiting cycle, not so much today.

“That roster came together about as well as we could have possibly hoped for, not only talent wise, but depth wise,” assistant coach Brian Michaelson said. “Ten years later, that’s what sticks out to me. It was the perfect mix of new guys, transfers and guys that had been in the program.”

With an interesting set of backstories accompanying many of the key players.

Healthy Karnowski

The biggest question mark was Karnowski’s health after his 2015-16 season lasted just five games due to a serious back injury.

The 285-pound center tried several treatment options but his condition deteriorated, He was finally diagnosed with a staph infection and promptly sent to the hospital. Doctors removed one disc, fused two others together, bracing the procedure with two screws and a plate.

Karnowski’s basketball career was in jeopardy, but he made methodical progress, received a medical redshirt year and was ready for the season opener against Utah Valley. He had 14 points and seven rebounds in that game and erased any doubts about his health when he torched No. 16 Arizona with 18 points in a December win at the Staples Center.

Few rarely joined international recruiting ace Lloyd on trips overseas, but the two ventured to Poland and then on to France to watch another recruit. They found a wonderful pizza place near Karnowski’s home. Shortly after, Few remembered staying in France at “kind of a hostel that anybody could just wander into your room. I’m not in Tommy’s league on those trips.”

They came back with a gentle giant who possessed a soft touch, elite passing ability, high basketball IQ and dominating presence on defense.

“I remember seeing him the first time and was like ‘holy moly’ with how big he was and how he moved for someone that size,” Few recalled. “He was coming off some really rough stuff (with his back). He was certainly a huge part of it (in 2016-17). He was a force.”

Karnowski only played 23 minutes per game but won the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Center of the Year award after averaging 12.2 points, 5.8 rebounds and nearly two assists per game.

On second thought

Williams-Goss earned All-Pac-12 recognition in each of his first two seasons at Washington, but the Huskies were just 33-30 overall and 14-22 in conference play.

He considered entering the draft before deciding to transfer in search of a program capable of making the NCAA Tournament. The Zags barely made his list and weren’t close to the top.

A candid conversation with Few and a recruiting visit altered Williams-Goss’s and Gonzaga’s future.

“I got on the phone with him and told him I’m not here to be your best friend,” Few said. “I’m 30 years older than you. You were known as a winner in high school. You have a real chance here. Why don’t you focus on stuff that really matters.

“I’ll be here for you and I’ll love you like I love the others that are here, but I’m not here to be your best friend.”

Williams-Goss was fully convinced during his recruiting visit, witnessing firsthand how the players got along, the program’s culture and the likelihood of experiencing the Big Dance for the first time in his career.

He quickly became a team leader. He set the tone defensively with a West Coast Conference-leading 64 steals and directed the offense with team-highs of 16.8 points and 4.4 assists. He was second in rebounding (6.0), sandwiched between Williams (6.4) and Collins (5.9).

The Oregon native was the primary option in crunch time – those were few and far between with most games decided by early in the second half – and routinely came though. He scored 24 of his 33 points in the second half – 11 in a row at one point – as Gonzaga held off BYU in Provo and posted three 20-point games in the NCAA Tournament. He tagged Washington with 23 points, five boards and five assists in a 27-point blowout.

Few pinpointed Williams-Goss’s communication skills.

“He really understood how important that is,” Few said. “(Recently) at practice, I was lecturing our current team about it. I don’t talk about Nigel as often now, I usually mention LeBron James (Few was an assistant on the USA’s gold-medal team at the Paris Olympics) because he was incredible with it. That 2017 team talked better than any team I’ve had.”

Same goes for defending.

“The size, rebounding and defense were real,” Michaelson said. “Those guys brought it every night to not have ups and downs.”

Home far from home

Williams, a bouncy 6-9 forward, as well as Collins and Tillie, gave Gonzaga well-rounded options in the frontcourt anchored by Karnowski. ‘J3’, as he was referred to by teammates and coaches, collected rebounds like his scholarship depended on it and was a capable scorer and versatile defender.

Williams, like Williams-Goss and Jeremy Jones, who was a two-sport athlete (basketball and football) at Rice before coming to GU, benefited from NCAA rules that required transfers to sit out one year.

GU’s track record with redshirts was established with the success stories of Kelly Olynyk and Kyle Wiltjer. Williams and Williams-Goss added their names to the growing list.

Williams had fine stats in his first two seasons at Missouri, but the Memphis native wanted to expand his game and line up in March Madness. Luckily for Gonzaga, his transfer options regionally were restricted by the SEC and Missouri so he studied schools far from home.

“Just initially I made a cold call,” Michaelson said. “We knew Wiltjer would be leaving that year (Williams) sat out (2015-16). J3 knew more about Gonzaga basketball than I expected and being able to sell that development program helped. Right away, he was receptive.”

That year, Williams and Collins shut down Arizona star forward Lauri Markkanen and South Dakota State scoring machine Mike Daum.

Mathews, Daniels connection

The final piece to the roster puzzle was Mathews, a proven 3-point shooter with 102 games under his belt in three seasons at Cal.

The 6-3 guard, eligible immediately as a grad transfer, had options, but Gonzaga had a huge head start. Mathews and his dad Phil, who faced GU for years as San Francisco’s coach from 1996-04, were close to then-Zags assistant Donny Daniels.

Mathews fit seamlessly. Arguably the team’s best pure shooter, he thrived in GU’s inside-out system, hitting a team-high 85 3s with 39.2% accuracy. The team made 38.2% on triples with Williams-Goss the lowest in the rotation at 36.8%.

Mathews delivered one of the biggest shots in program history, a 3-pointer with just under 1 minute left to spur the Zags past West Virginia in the Sweet 16.

“Jordan ended up being the ideal fit because he’s a coach’s kid and he was just a Zag,” Few said. “Just what we needed.”

Keeping their guards up

Perkins, who made his GU commitment live on a Denver TV station’s morning show in Aug. 2013, and Melson were major contributors to the 2017 Zags.

Perkins started at point guard in 2015-16 before shifting to more of a combo guard with Williams-Goss as the main ballhandler. Perkins hit nearly 40% of his 3-point attempts and added 3.1 assists per game.

He also started the sequence that led to Mathews’ clutch 3, rejecting 6-9 forward Nathan Adrian’s shot at the other end.

“Crazy Perk,” Few said with a chuckle. “He hit some big shots, he was a heck of a point guard. I used to always get on him, ‘You’re not a shot blocker, you’re going to have to take charges and strip guys down there.”

Melson often locked down one of the opponent’s top perimeter threats and chipped in points (7.2), assists (1.5) and 3-point shooting (39.1%).

Michaelson raved about Melson’s “defense, outside shooting and unselfishness.”

Freshmen phenoms

Gonzaga’s 2015-16 season could have been derailed by Karnowski’s injury but Wiltjer and Domantas Sabonis didn’t let that happen. The two forwards logged heavy minutes and combined to average 38 points and 18 rebounds as GU made the Sweet 16 and nearly the Elite Eight before stumbling late against Syracuse.

“With the uncertainty surrounding Przemek, the lack of bodies we had in the 2016 season and Domas and Wiltjer leaving, we knew the freshmen class had to be special,” Michaelson said.

Special might not be a strong enough word to describe the Zags’ incoming class: Collins, Tillie, Rui Hachimura, Zach Norvell and Jacob Larsen.

Collins was the headliner as a five-star addition. Collins and junior guard Melson typically were the first ones off the bench in an eight-man rotation that included the versatile Tillie.

Collins was fearless on the court in his first and only season as a Zag, He led the WCC with 69 blocks despite averaging just 17.3 minutes.

Collins cemented his draft status as a lottery pick with a 14-point, 13-rebound, 6-block effort in a Final Four win over South Carolina. Tillie gave GU another skilled big and he dropped in two free throws with 2.2 seconds left to seal the win over the Gamecocks.

Hachimura, early in the process of learning English and NCAA basketball, showed his enormous potential in blowouts. Norvell was sidelined with a knee injury. Larsen eventually left the program.

“How competitive those practices were was another thing I remember,” Michaelson said. “High level, big bodies going at it every day. The scout team had guys like Rui, Tillie, ‘Snacks’ (Norvell), Jones, Ryan Edwards, ‘BA” (Alberts). The last two went on to start (after transferring). We had great walk-ons (Rem Bakamus, Dustin Triano) that practiced hard and brought positivity and energy.”

Milestones and memories

Few and Michaelson knew Gonzaga had a quality team, but that came into sharper focus after the Zags edged Florida and No. 21 Iowa State in close games to win AdvoCare Invitational in Orlando and handled Arizona, Washington and Tennessee, the latter in Nashville.

“Orlando kind of made you go, ‘OK, we beat some nice teams, we could be somebody that is on the way to a high seed,’ ” Few said.

Gonzaga stacked up 29 straight wins, rising to No. 1 in late January, before falling to BYU in the regular-season finale. The Zags shook off that home loss with their third win over ranked Saint Mary’s, 74-56, for the WCC Tournament title.

Driven by an efficient offense and a stingy defense that ranked first nationally in field-goal percentage (36.5%) and 10th in scoring (61.5 per game), the Zags marched all the way into April with five NCAA Tournament wins, including tight victories over Northwestern, West Virginia and South Carolina.

But the win over South Carolina came at a cost as Williams-Goss tweaked an ankle injury and Karnowski battled blurry vision after getting poked in the eye.

In the title game, Williams-Goss scored GU’s last points, including a bucket that put the Zags ahead 65-63 just inside the two-minute mark. He rolled his ankle about 30 seconds later. The Tar Heels scored the game’s final eight points for a 71-65 win.

“Going back and watching some of those foul calls, almost in some ways both ways,” Few reflected. “North Carolina had a great front line, too. I don’t know who got the idea to start fouling everybody out. For Zach Collins … if he plays 10 more minutes in that game we win, I’m not going to say easy, and he picked up some of the cheapest ones.

“On my son Joe’s iPad, he had a picture of the Carolina guy (Kennedy Meeks with 50 seconds left) laying on the ball out of bounds on there for five years or something. I’d have to walk by it. Good lord, do I have to look at that (missed call) all the time?”

Gonzaga didn’t cut down the nets, but reaching the Final Four and national championship game validated the program’s place among the nation’s elite.

“I’m not a receipt kind of guy, but it was for my own sanity or just looking back with all the opportunities I had,” he said. “I tried to explain to people on the other side of the phone that I think we can win a national championship, go to a Final Four. And they’d look at me like I was kind of crazy.

“It made me feel like I wasn’t crazy.”

Crazy might be an apt description of the difference between assembling the 2017 roster and the process in today’s NIL, transfer-heavy landscape.

“It’s just a whole new world,” Few said. “It was more about who was patient enough to redshirt and sit and wait their turn. That’s not happening in this day and age.”

Gonzaga.title: At 7-4, Purdue's Daniel Jacobsen is literally, figuratively a huge part of Gonzaga's game plan | Key matchup
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – Déjà vu? More like déjà Purdue.

In 2024, Mark Few was asked to summarize the challenge his Gonzaga team faced with top-seeded Purdue and 7-foot-3 center Zach Edey standing in the way of an Elite Eight appearance at the NCAA Tournament.

“He’s an entity you just don’t see,” Few said of Edey, who’d go on to collect his second consecutive Naismith Trophy weeks after hurting Gonzaga for 27 points and 14 rebounds in Purdue’s 80-68 win.

Two years later, Few finds himself coming back to a similar term with Purdue back on the calendar for Monday’s season opener at T-Mobile Arena (4:30 p.m., TNT) and another massive human occupying the center position for Matt Painter and the Boilermakers.

Few’s description of 7-foot-4, 250-pound Purdue junior Daniel Jacobsen?

“Skilled and just kind of that entity you don’t face every night in college basketball,” the Gonzaga coach said Friday. “I don’t even know if we’ll face it again after this.”

Maybe not until the next time Gonzaga links up with Purdue.

Under Painter, the Boilermakers have cycled through skilled, imposing 7-footers like few others in the sport. Purdue rode 7-foot AJ Hammons early in the coach’s tenure, had four solid seasons with 7-2 Isaac Haas, recruited 7-3 BYU transfer Matt Haarms to replace Haas and hit a gold mine with the 7-3 Edey.

Jacobsen, the tallest of the bunch, slides into the center role vacated by 6-11 Oscar Cluff, the former Washington State and South Dakota State center who averaged 10.5 points and 7.6 rebounds during Purdue’s run to the Elite Eight.

Purdue’s great centers didn’t get by on measurables alone, though, and Jacobsen is stepping into a big role for the first time in his career after averaging just 13 minutes and six points as a freshman and sophomore.

Even for a center who will take on a daunting Big Ten schedule months from now, the challenges won’t get much bigger than Monday’s in Vegas.

Gonzaga is debuting a frontcourt of 6-foot-10 Braden Huff and 7-foot-1 Massamba Diop. Purdue could counter with 7-foot-4 Jacobsen and 6-foot-7 Caden Pierce, Huff’s longtime friend and former Glenbard West High School teammate.

Last week, Diop and Jacobsen were both named to the preseason Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Center Award watch list while Huff and Pierce were two of the 20 players on the Karl Malone Power Forward Award watch list.

Huff’s familiarity with both Purdue frontcourt starters could play a role in Monday’s matchup. The fifth-year Gonzaga senior has been close with Pierce since fifth grade and he recently got to know Jacobsen, another Chicago area native, during offseason workouts sponsored by Priority Sports. Huff, Pierce and Jacobsen are all clients of the Chicago-based agency.

“He’s a good dude, excited to compete against him,” Huff said of Jacobsen. “Obviously he’s huge and he’s got nice touch around the rim. He even will go out and shoot it a little bit. And at that length, he blocks shots and is good defensively around the rim, too. So poses a good challenge for us but excited to go out and compete against those guys and it’s a good test for us first game.”

It’s not totally clear how the four frontcourt players will match up. If Purdue elects to go size on size, Jacobsen likely starts on Diop. That could leave the Boilermakers vulnerable against Huff, who poses a bigger offensive threat than his sophomore teammate. Either way, Pierce will be at a height disadvantage, giving up roughly 5 inches to Huff and 7 inches to Diop. That could favor for Purdue at the other end, where the Boilermakers will look to stretch the floor using Pierce as a cutter and 3-point shooter.

The bench bigs should factor in, too. For Gonzaga, that’s 6-10 Spanish forward Izan Almansa. Purdue could rely on 6-11 redshirt sophomore Raleigh Burgess and/or 6-foot-9 French senior Enzo Shahrvin.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women expect challenge from experienced North Dakota State team
Gonzaga.summary:
When the Gonzaga women’s basketball players step on the court Monday at McCarthey Athletic Center, forgive them if they feel like they’re looking at a team similar to themselves.

In many ways, the Zags will be.

Gonzaga takes on North Dakota State on the first day college men’s and women’s teams may play games. Tipoff is at 6 p.m.

The teams met in Gonzaga’s 2025-26 season opener in Fargo, North Dakota – a game the Zags won 81-66.

NDSU went on to win the Summit League championship and finish 29-5 overall. The Bison return five starters and eight letterwinners.

Sound familiar? Gonzaga returns all five starters and five other key returners off a team that was 24-10, won the West Coast Conference title and conference tournament and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

“They’re really, really good,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said. “They’re just as veteran as we are.”

In the opener a year ago, Gonzaga led 60-38 through three quarters before the Bison pulled closer in the final period. Four Zags finished in double-figure scoring, led by Allie Turner with 18 points on 4-of-5 shooting from 3-point range. Zeryhia Aokuso had 14 points, Lauren Whittaker, in her first collegiate game, had 13 and nine rebounds in 18 minutes and Ines Bettencourt added 12 points and four assists.

The Zags will have to keep many eyes on NDSU 6-foot-3 senior forward Avery Koenen, who had 17 to lead the Bison against GU.

Like Whittaker, Koenen is on the Becky Hammon Mid-Major Player of the Year preseason watch list. She was the Summit League Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year. She’s been tabbed as the league’s preseason POY.

“(Koenen) is one of the best in the country,” Fortier said. “She was one of five players in the country who were the Defensive Player of the Year and the Player of the Year. They have really good guards around her.”

Koenen led NDSU in scoring last year, averaging 19.4 points and 10.8 rebounds. She was the only player in the country last year to average at least 19 points, 10 rebounds and shoot 63% or better.

“They’re kind of like us outside of Spokane, right?” Fortier said. “Everybody in Spokane knows how good they are, but other people don’t. We’re going to have to defend their guards who are tough and gritty. They’re feisty. They can shoot it from the perimeter. They’re athletic. Koenen is an issue that you have to address at all times when she’s on the court.”

Fortier says Koenen wins most one-on-one battles with forwards.

“So we’re going to have to dig in,” Fortier said.

The game is the first of three straight home games for the Zags. GU welcomes Idaho, an NCAA Tournament qualifier a year ago, on Friday and UC Riverside visits on Sunday.

Gonzaga.title: On BFR, self-belief and the road back to basketball for Gonzaga's Braden Huff: 'He was disciplined'
Gonzaga.summary:
Before returning to Spokane in August, Braden Huff swung by Achieve Orthopedic Sports Institute in the Chicago area to drop off a handwritten letter and photograph for Brandi Hosford. He wanted to extend gratitude and appreciation to the physical therapist who logged hundreds of hours working to get the Gonzaga forward back on the court after dislocating his left kneecap.

It was a high-character move that wasn’t necessarily of character for the easygoing, even-mannered Huff. He signed his name at the bottom of the letter and attached a photo of him and Hosford, who volunteered at the annual basketball camp Huff puts on every summer in his hometown to support a local food pantry.

Not that Hosford would’ve had any trouble identifying where, or who, the letter came from.

“It said he was really thankful for rehab and that BFR sucks, but it works really well,” Hosford said earlier this week. “The response that was on it is definitely, totally Braden.”

BFR, or Blood Flow Restriction, is the specialized rehabilitation technique Hosford used to aid and accelerate Huff’s return to the court. It’s impossible to recap Huff’s rehab journey without at least one mention of the three-letter acronym, as long as the forward isn’t within earshot when you do.

“You kind of wrap it around your upper thigh and it restricts your blood flow and it feels like you’re lifting super heavy weights when you’re doing lighter and it was no fun,” Huff said. “That was probably my least favorite.”

“I would be shocked if that didn’t come up,” father Alec Huff said. “He didn’t like that whatsoever.”

“I knew Braden was going to say that,” Hosford said. “I think he’s got a love/hate relationship with it, right? He loves to hate it, but hates that he loves it.”

There’s less confusion about Huff’s feelings toward the game that was promptly taken from him in January, when a routine practice play turned into a freak accident, ending an All-American-caliber season 17 games short of the finish line and hurling the forward into an eight-month rehab assignment.

“You go from kind of 100 to zero,” Huff said.

The forward’s slow, steady climb back to 100 began the next day. First, the knee surgery. Then the daily physical therapy sessions and dreaded encounters with Blood Flow Restriction. Huff wasn’t able to move on his left leg for a few months but once he ditched his crutches, stationary shooting workouts followed shortly after. Huff made 100 free throws every day with assistant Brian Michaelson before moving to the next phase of his recovery plan.

“We’ve all spent a lot of time with him and know him and who he is at his core really well,” Michaelson said. “From the minute he went down, it was exactly how we all envisioned him attacking his rehab. He had a great spirit to him, he was disciplined, he was patient.”

Best of all, he’s been hardened by the adversity.

Hard decisions

Alec and Stacey Huff got the phone call on the afternoon of Jan. 15. They were making a long, familiar haul from Chicago to Spokane for a game at Washington State the following day. The Huffs don’t have the advantage of proximity residing in the Midwest, but they travel to every major nonconference game and hit a variety of others throughout the year. It’s a running joke that Stacey is the family’s unofficial “travel agent.”

But the Huffs put future plans on ice when their son called the day before WSU. He didn’t want to alarm them, but there’d been an incident at practice. Gonzaga didn’t have an official diagnosis, but the forward couldn’t bear weight on his left leg and things weren’t looking good for the following day in Pullman, let alone the weeks or months to come.

“He never wants us to worry too much, so when he called us … he didn’t really maybe let on to the severity of it initially, but it became pretty clear pretty fast,” Alec said.

The Zags scaled back the intensity in their final practice before a key West Coast Conference rivalry game in Pullman. Huff was playing post-position defense when he took a normal step and immediately noticed an abnormal sensation in his knee.

It was a move he’d performed hundreds if not thousands of times in practices and games earlier in the season. He’d taken bigger physical gambles in higher-stakes environments with no repercussions. He brawled with Michigan’s lottery-pick littered frontcourt and hardly emerged with a scratch.

So how could a non-descript, non-contact play during a glorified walkthrough be what suspended a magnificent junior season?

“A lot of times a non-contact ACL or some of these non-contact things that happen without any outside forces sometimes, I describe it as like a neural mistime,” head Gonzaga athletic trainer Josh Therrien said. “When you’re walking down the stairs and you think there’s one more and your body’s expecting something and there’s actually not, so you nearly fall. The nervous system is prepared for something to happen and there’s sort of this mistime that happens.”

When the injury occurred, Huff was leading the country in 2-point field goal efficiency (72.2%) and total field goals made (145). A month earlier, he’d registered a career-high 37 points against Campbell – a clinic in scoring efficiency that saw the forward finish 16 of 18 from the field.

Postseason all-conference honors were the bare minimum for someone averaging 17.8 points and only gaining steam in WCC play. Huff was squarely in the mix for the WCC Most Outstanding Player honor that ultimately went to close friend and teammate Graham Ike. All-American honors wouldn’t have been a stretch.

Gonzaga provided a timeline of four to eight weeks, cautiously clinging to hope Huff would be available in some capacity for meaningful games in March. The Zags probably wouldn’t get the version of Huff that dizzied defenders with spin moves, converted floaters at an automatic clip and hit opponents with hook shot after hook shot. But maybe he could provide one quality shift each half. Force NCAA Tournament opponents to consider him in pregame scouting reports. Supply just one of those patented floaters to help the Zags through a cold offensive stretch.

“Any sports medicine mentors of mine have said never say never, never say always,” said Therrien, who stayed in constant communication with Huff, his parents, agent and GU’s coaches to discuss the best course of action.

The cloudy conversations became more straightforward when Texas clipped Gonzaga in the NCAA’s Round of 32, giving Huff a clear runway to recover and zero pressure to test his knee anytime soon.

“I think after that,” Huff said, “there was obviously no rush because there was no more games until this weekend.”

Getting behind BFR

Therrien worked with Huff’s family to facilitate medical treatment in the Chicago area, allowing the forward to work with a nationally-renowned orthopedic surgeon and recover in the quiet comfort of his Glen Ellyn, Illinois, home.

Huff’s operation was done by Dr. Brian Cole, the head team physician for the NBA’s Chicago Bulls, a managing partner of Midwest Orthopaedics at Rush University Medical Center and potentially one of only a handful of orthopedic surgeons in the country with his own Wikipedia page.

“We’ve had a previous history and relationship with the surgeon he did see, it just happened to be near his hometown,” Therrien said. “If he was Florida, we probably still would refer to the surgeon we did.”

Cole had a working relationship with Hosford, who previously knew Huff through her other venture, a training company called Athlete Advantage Performance Labs. Post-surgery, Hosford took the reins on Huff’s rehabilitation, seeing him four times per week, anywhere from two to three hours per day.

Huff’s anxiety level driving to visits with Hosford varied day to day. Twice a week, she had the Gonzaga forward hooked up to a BFR cuff – which was wrapped around his lower thigh, just above the targeted knee area – from anywhere between 20-45 minutes, with varied rest between sets.

Medical journals trace the earliest uses of the technique to Japan in the 1960s. The cuff acts like a tourniquet to reduce, or occlude, blood flow to certain parts of the body, promoting muscular growth and cardiovascular function.

“So essentially you’re simulating an environment of max effort,” Hosford said. “I ran track in college, so at the end of running an all-out 400-meter dash where you’re crossing the finish line and your legs feel so locked you can’t move, the BFR essentially creates that same environment but you can just use bodyweight or really light weights. So it’s great because you’re kind of tricking the body into thinking it’s maxing out without actually needing to.”

Early on, Hosford ran Huff through a variety of basic exercises with the application of BFR: long arc quads, straight leg raises, bridges, step ups, etc. It eventually progressed to standard weight-room movements like split squats, back squat, step-ups, calf raises, machine-based exercises, knee extensions and hamstring curls.

Then there were the energy-draining cardio sessions. BFR can be beneficial under VO2 max, a marker that measures volume of oxygen consumed during exercise, so Huff would routinely strap on the cuff before treadmill work, biking segments or sled push/pull workouts.

“It’s kind of a cheat code where you can maintain your body without overworking it between playing games,” Hosford said.

Late in the summer, Hosford she had news that would perk her client up. Huff was done with the BFR portion of his summer rehab stint … after one more set of knee extensions. The issue? Huff was adamant he’d completed all four sets. In disbelief, he looked at his dad, looked at another strength coach and then back at Hosford.

“He goes ‘No, she’s lying,’ ” Hosford recalled. “I was like ‘No, you have one more set. We always have four sets.’ And he goes, ‘Are there cameras? Where are the facility cameras? I need to pull, we need to see. I’ve already done four sets.’ ”

Two weeks later, Huff and Hosford revisited the scene at his summer camp.

“He’s like, ‘No take me through the whole series of events of how we got there and how you think I missed a set,’ ” Hosford said, adding that Huff eventually conceded but not before another hard-fought debate.

No-lose proposition

Huff’s gentle, unassuming personality clashes with a competitive gene likely passed down from his parents.

Six years ago during the COVID-19 lockdown, Alec suggested the family get fresh air and go out to the driveway for pickup hoops. Older sister Taylor had grown less inclined to take part in those outings because of the growing skill and height gap between Braden and everyone else in the family. But, provided trash talk stay at a minimum, she was in.

Alec proposed a rule: the first to jaw at another family member had to sprint to the end of the driveway and back. He was also the first to break, taking Braden to the hole on an early out of bounds play and subsequently letting his DI-bound son have an earful.

“I realize I’m the issue,” Alec said. “So I start sprinting up and down the driveway.”

Pickleball, card games, basketball, board games. It’s all the same. Huff doesn’t take loss kindly and doesn’t let go of things easily. During one family trip, Stacey tried to bend the rules in a Monopoly game, suggesting she and another player go in on a property together, enraging her son in the process.

“Braden just totally had a fit and gave up, like you can’t do that, you’re cheating,” Alec said. “That’s kind of the way it works in our house. … That’s just who he is at his core.”

So one can only imagine what the family couch looked like on Feb. 4.

Gonzaga was at Portland in what most expected would be a WCC walkover. Huff was still in Illinois, watching in the living room with his parents – an experience that was admittedly unusual for all parties. The Pilots raced out to an early lead and pulled off the miracle of miracles, hanging on for an 87-80 win.

“He didn’t like watching that one at all,” Alec recalled. “He’s certainly not yelling at his guys, he’s almost just befuddled, like what’s going on here?”

The final act

Progress reports on Huff post-rehab indicate there’s been little to no drop-off in the smooth lefty’s game.
