“B-Huff, when I first came here and watched him work out, probably saw him miss one floater the whole workout,” Gonzaga guard and Houston transfer Isiah Harwell said. “That was crazy to watch.”

In the category of things even crazier? How Huff held up through low-post duels with a three-time NBA All-Star late in the offseason. Domantas Sabonis, the NBA’s leader in rebounding average (16.2 rpg), dropped by Gonzaga’s facilities to get a few final offseason workouts in and visit with former college coaches before returning to the Sacramento Kings.

“Not saying I was going crazy, but playing against him, competing against him, I feel like holding my own just felt great,” said Huff, noting Sabonis was also coming off a rehab assignment from his own knee injury. “I think that felt good for my confidence knowing this is a guy who plays at the highest level obviously … being able to compete against a guy like that and hold my own, feel good about it, I think was good for my confidence.”

It was an accurate characterization, too.

“B-Huff did his thing,” teammate Davis Fogle verified.

There’s no evidence to suggest Huff has skipped a beat on the court – 19 points and 11 rebounds against an athletic Arkansas frontcourt would support the exact opposite – and those around the program believe he’s in the best physical shape he’s been in since arriving in 2022 as a tall, gangly freshman.

“His leg strength I think is the best it’s ever been and obviously coming back from a leg injury, that’s so important,” assistant coach Brian Michaelson said. “But the way he’s moving, his leg strength, the balance between his legs both being similar in size, similar in strength, those were the things that were really important as he came back from this.”

Apparent upper-body gains have raised eyebrows, too. During Kraziness in the Kennel, ESPN analyst and event emcee Sean Farnham inquired about practice photos that surfaced last month depicting the forward’s biceps and shoulders as more chiseled than usual. Humbly, Huff tried to cast the images off as “AI.”

Not entirely true.

Partial credit goes to Stacey, who kept her son fueled with heaping meal portions during his time in Illinois. Steak, chicken piccata, chicken and biscuits and tuna were all on the menu.

“It was kind of crazy,” Alec said. “He would go either here or to train downtown and come back and his mother would have like a full dinner for him at noon.”

But Huff has also made serious strides with strength coach Travis Knight, revealing five years ago he could barely do one weighted pull-up on a resistance-based machine Gonzaga players use. The forward easily knocks out five to seven at a time now, usually performing four or five sets per session.

“Those got a lot easier,” Huff said. “It’s cool to recall on that growth and see the changes over time.”

There’s been growth in other areas, too. The once-timid Huff has emerged from his shell to become Gonzaga’s vocal leader, inheriting a key role on a team that has just two returning contributors.

“I think his body’s matured, definitely matured and he’s got that kind of senior confidence about him,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said. “He understands he’s got to be more assertive and more vocal.”

Huff’s next act will be his final one in a Gonzaga jersey. Notably, he received zero preseason AP All-American votes despite posting a better 2025-26 scoring average than 17 of the 24 players who collected at least one vote and a better field goal percentage than all of them.

That didn’t go unnoticed.

“All that stuff, you kind of take note of,” Huff said. “Everybody kind of sees all that stuff, whether they admit to it or not.”

The last 10 months have felt more like 10 years, but Huff now sits roughly 24 hours from his long-awaited return, a 4:30 p.m. tipoff against Purdue at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas on Monday that should induce a variety of feelings and emotions from the family members, friends, high school coaches and Braden Huff Basketball Camp counselors planning to turn out.

“For sure it will be emotional,” Alec Huff said. “He’s worked his tail off to get back and the last year was really tough for him. I think he was devastated when that injury happened. … I guess all of that wraps into yeah, it’ll probably be a little emotional for us but in a good way.”

Gonzaga.title: Pac-12 preview: New-look conference should provide stiff challenges, hostile road arenas
Gonzaga.summary:
On Sept. 16, Utah State announced the school had sold out tickets for Gonzaga’s inaugural trip to Dee Glen Smith Spectrum. That wouldn’t necessarily be news – certainly not Gonzaga’s first time drawing a standing room-only crowd on the road – but the announcement arrived two full weeks before the Pac-12 Conference released its schedule, meaning more than 10,000 fans purchased tickets without knowing a concrete date for the Jan. 21 matchup.

Gonzaga can expect bigger crowds and more robust challenges in the new conference, which should test the Bulldogs top-to-bottom in a way the West Coast Conference didn’t and help Mark Few’s avoid the resume dings that were often inevitable in January and February.

The reimagined Pac-12 may not be ready to compete with the SEC, Big Ten, Big 12, ACC and Big East on Selection Sunday, but this new group of nine isn’t lacking credentials.

Gonzaga and San Diego State bring three combined national championship appearances over the last nine years with 31 combined NCAA Tournament victories sprinkled in during that span. Utah State is in the middle of the school’s best run, punching six NCAA tickets over the last eight seasons, including each of the last four. Boise State made three straight March Madness trips before recent misses and Colorado State has been exceptional in its own right, qualifying in 2022, 2024 and 2025. Oregon State and Washington State both made semirecent NCAA appearances under the Pac-12’s old flag.

This new-look Pac-12 might have been a candidate to get three teams into the previous NCAA Tournament, but the expanded 76-team bracket provides a pathway to one or two additional bids.

Regardless, college hoops fans out West should have plenty of dates to circle on the new Pac-12 calendar – not just the one taking place Jan. 21 in Logan, Utah.

1. Gonzaga

Coach: Mark Few (772-156), 28th year at Gonzaga

2025-26 record: 31-4. WCC: 16-2, tied-first

Key newcomers: C Massamba Diop (7-1, 230), G Isiah Harwell (6-6, 220), G Nathan De Sousa (6-2, 192), F Izan Almansa (6-10, 200/eligibility pending), G Xaivian Lee (6-4, 185), F Chauncey Wiggins (6-11, 225/eligibility pending), G Javon Bennett (5-10, 165/eligibility pending)

Key losses: F Graham Ike, G Tyon Grant-Foster, G Jalen Warley, F Emmanuel Innocenti, G Mario Saint-Supery, G Adam Miller, G Braeden Smith, C Ismaila Diagne

Outlook: Despite the various curveballs this offseason has tossed their way, the Zags are still the favorites – considerable favorites, maybe – to capture a Pac-12 crown next spring. They’ve assembled one of the country’s top frontcourts, blending Braden Huff’s offensive touch with Massamba Diop’s rim protection. This should be a second-weekend team with a Final Four ceiling if Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett and Chauncey Wiggins stay/become eligible.

2. Utah State

Coach: Ben Jacobson (397-259), 1st year at Utah State

2025-26 record: 29-7. Mountain West: 15-5, first

Key newcomers: Dallin Hall (6-4, 200/eligibility pending), Connor Turnbull (6-11, 225), AJ Bates (6-4, 200), Solomon Callaghan (6-2, 195), Will Hornseth (6-9, 235), Collin Mulholland (6-11, 240)

Key losses: G MJ Collins Jr., G Drake Allen, G Kolby King, F Garry Clark, F Adlan Elamin, G Elijah Perryman

Outlook: Constant coaching turnover hasn’t impacted the Aggies, who’ve been to four consecutive NCAA Tournaments under three different coaches. Utah State has a solid chance to get there again under Ben Jacobson, who made five NCAA appearances over 20 seasons at Northern Iowa. The Aggies will lean heavily on veteran forward Mason Falslev, the favorite to earn Pac-12 MVP honors if the award doesn’t go to a Gonzaga player. Frontcourt mate and reigning Mountain West Sixth Man of the Year Karson Templin is another solid all-conference candidate.

3. San Diego State

Coach: Brian Dutcher (220-79), 10th year at San Diego State

2025-26 record: 22-11. Mountain West: 13-6, second

Key newcomers: G Chance Gladden (6-4, 192), G Isaiah Sy (6-6, 200), F Bear Cherry (6-10, 270), G David Torresani (6-2, 168), G Zach White (6-5, 208), F Luca Vincini (6-10, 242)

Key losses: F Magoon Gwath, F Pharaoh Compton, G Miles Byrd, G BJ Davis, G Taj DeGourville, G Reese Dixon-Waters, F Miles Heide

Outlook: This won’t be Brian Dutcher’s strongest roster on paper, but we’ll give the benefit of the doubt to a coach who’s been part of four Mountain West regular-season or tournament championships and six NCAA Tournament appearances since taking over for Steve Fisher. Elzie Harrington, the team’s only returning starter, is a proficient 3-point shooter, but the Aztecs may also require a lot from transfers Chance Gladden (Boston U), Bear Cherry (Sacramento State) and Isaiah Sy (Oregon State), especially in the wake of Nick Anderson’s offseason knee injury.

4. Oregon State

Coach: Justin Joyner (0-0), 1st season at Oregon State

2025-26 record: 17-16. WCC: 9-9, tie-fourth

Key newcomers: F Jackson Rasmussen (6-9, 211), G Legend Smiley (6-5, 188), G Daniel Freitag (6-2, 192), F DeShawn Gory (6-6, 169), C Xavion Staton (7-1, 224), G Chris Johnson (6-5, 189), C Dennis Evans (7-2, 231)

Key losses: F Isaiah Sy, G Dez White, F Johan Munch, C Yaak Yaak, F Jorge Diaz Graham, F Olavi Suutela

Outlook: Justin Joyner, a national title-winning assistant with years of experience building scouting reports for Gonzaga, takes over Oregon State’s program after Wayne Tinkle’s tenure ended. Joyner lacks head-coaching experience, but he’s assembled a roster that looks talented enough on paper to compete with the top half of the Pac-12. Program veteran Josiah Lake II brings leadership and ball-handling, while transfers DeShawn Gory (Fresno State) and Daniel Freitag (Buffalo) have a chance to lead the Beavers in scoring. Similar to the Michigan team Joyner worked for last season, OSU should be massive up front with three 7-footers on this roster.

5. Colorado State

Coach: Ali Farokhmanesh (21-13), second season at Colorado State

2025-26 record: 21-13. Mountain West: 11-9, seventh

Key newcomers: G Justin Menard (6-3, 185), F Jaden Ghoreishi (6-9, 215), Amondo Miller Jr. (6-7, 195)

Key losses: F Brandon Rechsteiner, G Jevin Muniz, F Augustinas Kiudulas

Outlook: The Rams lose their top scorer from a year ago, but return players who ranked second, third, fourth, sixth and seventh in points per game. It’s a level of retention that’s hard to come by in the current college basketball climate and one of the primary reasons Ali Farokhmanesh’s group might be a step ahead of others in the Pac-12 when the regular season begins. Marist transfer Justin Menard slides into the starting lineup next to a quartet of returners that includes three double-digit scorers in Kyle Jorgensen (11.5 ppg), Carey Booth (10.7 ppg) and Josh Pascarelli (10.2 ppg). Spokane’s Jaden Ghoreishi could see minutes off the bench as a freshman.

6. Boise State

Coach: Leon Rice (336-189), 17th season at Boise State

2025-26 record: 20-12. Mountain West: 12-8, tie-fifth

Key newcomers: F Dovydas Butka (6-9, 225), G Ty Rodgers (6-6, 205), G Lamar Washington (6-4, 210/eligibility pending), G Damari Wheeler-Thomas (6-0, 190).

Key losses: F Javan Buchanan, F Drew Fielder, G Dylan Andrews, F Andrew Meadow, F Dominic Parolin

Outlook: Former Gonzaga assistant Leon Rice faces a tall task replacing Boise State’s four double-digit scorers from a year ago, especially after an offseason injury to Ty Rodgers sidelined the Illinois transfer indefinitely. Campbell’s Dovydas Butka is a nightly double-double threat while North Dakota State transfer Damari Wheeler-Thomas is expected to take on primary ball-handling duties. Returning reserves Julian Bowie and Aginaldo Neto both had 20-plus point performances in recent exhibitions against Idaho and Washington. If eligible, 5-in-5 Georgia Tech transfer Lamar Washington has a chance to be one of Boise State’s top scorers, rebounders and facilitators.

7. Texas State

Coach: Terrence Johnson (107-81), seventh season at Texas State

2025-26 record: 19-13. Sun Belt: 11-7, tie-second

Key newcomers: G Quel’Ron House (6-0, 180), G KJ Younger (6-4, 218), F Ronald Jessamy (6-8, 220), G Caleb Steger (6-5, 180)

Key losses: G Franck Emmou, G Jaelyn Lee, C Tay Knox, G Deke Thompson, F Isaiah Barganier, G Cameron Simpson

Outlook: DJ Hall is one of the best-kept secrets in midmajor basketball and should be at the top of every Texas State scouting report this season after averaging 15.6 points, 7.7 rebounds and 1.4 steals as a freshman. The Bobcats have continuity beyond Hall, though, and managed to bring back second-leading scorer Mark Drone (14.2 ppg), assists/steals leader Kaden Gumbs (3.0 apg, 1.9 spg) and guard Dimp Pernell, who made 40.6% of his 3-pointers before a season-ending injury. Southern Illinois transfer Quel’Ron House will have a chance to be one of Texas State’s top two-way players.

8. Washington State

Coach: David Riley (93-73), third season at Washington State

2025-26 record: 12-20. WCC: 7-11, eighth

Key newcomers: G Lazerek Houston (6-0, 155), F Ronnie Harrison (6-8, 210), F Fraser Roxburgh (6-7, 215), G Sebastian Akins (6-2, 175), F Ladji Dembele (6-8, 255), G Jaylen Harrell (6-5, 210), F Tyler Kropp (6-9, 230), G Jamari Phillips (6-4, 190), G R.J. Jones, 6-2, 189 (2.6 ppg, 0.4 rpg).

Key losses: G Ace Glass, G Rihards Vavers, F ND Okafor, F Eeemeli Yalaho, G Tomas Thrastarson, G Jerone Morton, F Emmanuel Ugbo, G Kase Wynott, G Adria Rodriguez, G Parker Gerrits.

Outlook: The Cougars lost 98.9% of their scoring from 2025-26 – only Dio Blakely’s 0.8 points per game return – and are easily the most challenging team to handicap a year later. With an all-new starting lineup and rotation, it’s wise not to read too deeply into WSU’s 92-64 exhibition loss at New Mexico, but also means David Riley’s squad could face growing pains through a challenging nonconference schedule that sends the Cougs outside of Pullman 11 times in November and December. Division II standout Lazerek Houston and East Texas A&M Ronnie Harrison both hit double digits on efficient shooting in the exhibition loss, with Harrison scoring 23 in Sunday’s 84-80 exhibition win at Washington.

9. Fresno State

Coach: Vance Walberg (33-80), third season at Fresno State

2025-26 record: 13-19. Mountain West: 7-13, 10th

Key newcomers: G Dragos Lungu (6-6, 180), G Ross Candelino (6-5, 198), F Bradey Henige (7-0, 240), G Brian Amuneke (6-5, 184), C Baye Fall (6-11, 205), G Quentin Rhymes (6-6, 195), G KJ Perry (6-3, 180)

Key losses: G Jake Heidbreder, F Deshawn Gory, F Jac Mani, G David Douglas Jr., C Wilson Jacques, G Zaon Collins, G Cameron Faas, C Gasper Kocevar, G Bastien Rieber

Outlook: Washington State and Fresno State face the biggest rebuilds and not surprisingly are the teams occupying the final two spots in our predictions. But there could be a sizable gap between the Cougars and Bulldogs, who are separated by 60 spots in Ken Pomeroy’s preseason ratings. Fresno State lost every contributor from last year and could rely heavily on guards Dragos Lungu, a 13.8 ppg scorer at UT Martin, and Ross Candelino, who averaged 11.2 ppg at Libscomb to lead them in the scoring column. The Bulldogs will have to turn things around after settling for a 19-45 record over Vance Walberg’s first two seasons.

Gonzaga.title: Diop Named to Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Award Watch List
Gonzaga.summary: SPRINGFIELD, Mass. – Gonzaga's Massamba Diop was named to the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Award Watch List. The Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame announced the 20 watch-list candidates Friday.

Gonzaga.summary: SPOKANE, Wash. – Gonzaga opens the regular season against No. 24 Purdue in the TNT Hall of Fame Series in T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas.

Gonzaga.title: Massamba Diop becomes third Gonzaga player named to preseason positional watch list
Gonzaga.summary:
A member of Gonzaga’s starting frontcourt has been named to a preseason positional watch list for the third time in as many days.

Sophomore center Massamba Diop was one of 20 players included Friday on the watch list for the Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Award, joining teammates Davis Fogle and Braden Huff, who were respectively named to watch lists for the Julius Erving Award and Karl Malone Award earlier this week.

Diop, a coveted transfer from Arizona State, committed to Gonzaga over St. John’s in April and is expected solidify one of the best frontcourt units in the country with his rim protection and athleticism.

A native of Rufisque, Senegal, Diop averaged 13.6 points, 5.8 rebounds and 2.1 blocks per game playing under Bobby Hurley at ASU. He started in all 33 games for the Sun Devils, shooting 56.9% from the field. Diop was one of the Big 12’s top shot blockers as a freshman, ranking second behind Kansas’ Flory Bidunga in total blocks (69). That number also ranked third among college basketball freshmen.

Diop scored a season-high 22 points for ASU in a 104-76 loss to BYU and had 10 rebounds in two Big 12 games, against Cincinnati and Baylor. He registered a season-high seven blocks during ASU’s 95-89 home loss to Colorado.

Diop struggled with foul trouble in Gonzaga’s 76-72 exhibition loss at Arkansas on Saturday, scoring just four points with five rebounds, but the 7-foot-1 center fared slightly better on Wednesday against NAIA Lewis-Clark State, scoring eight second-half points for 10 in the game to go with five rebounds, one block and one steal.

The watch list also includes Arizona’s Motiejus Krivas, Creighton’s Oswin Erhunmwunse, Duke’s Patrick Ngongba II, Florida’s Rueben Chinyelu, Florida State’s Marcis Ponder, Illinois’ Tomislav Ivisic, Iowa’s Andrew McKeever, Kentucky’s Malachi Moreno, Louisville’s Bidunga, Marquette’s Sananda Fru, Maryland’s Pharrel Payne, Miami’s Somo Cyril, Michigan’s Moustapha Thiam, Purdue’s Daniel Jacobsen, SMU’s Jaden Toombs, Texas’ Matas Vokietaitis, Villanova’s Luigi Suigo, Virginia’s Johann Grunloh and Wisconsin’s Nolan Winter.

Gonzaga.title: How Gonzaga women have bucked the revolving door trend in new era: 'We recruit uniquely'
Gonzaga.summary:
In a time when a premium is placed on player retention and roster rebuilding, we give you the antithesis: Gonzaga women’s basketball.

At the same time college basketball seems to shift with each change in wind direction, Gonzaga coach Lisa Fortier longs for the old days. Back when building a roster began and ended with high school freshmen.

COVID-19 and the recent 5-for-5 eligibility change has thrown wrenches into the formula in which Gonzaga was built on.

Gonzaga desires that its foundation includes high school players. When the program started making a name for itself in the mid -2000s, the Zags were signing high school players. Before Fortier and continuing during her watch, Gonzaga has followed that formula. Recruit and sign high school athletes, take time to develop them and ultimately reap the benefits.

“We recruit uniquely,” Fortier said. “We’ve never been the group that just amasses talent. We’ve tried to find the right pieces to fit in together. And there is some movement … you can only control so much of that. But we take good care of them. We surround them with people you want to hang out with.”

Fortier has seen it up close for two decades. She’s beginning her 13th season as the Zags’ head coach and 20th overall.

It’s not a coincidence that many programs across the nation have had to eschew the once -traditional means of developing and sustaining their teams – through the signing and development of high school players – for quick fixes brought on by graduation or losses in the transfer portal – in hopes of remaining competitive and not falling behind the winning curve.

Gonzaga has stayed ahead of the curve.

Go back two decades when Gonzaga came on the mid-major scene and started giving teams from power conferences all they could handle. The Bulldogs had an occasional transfer back then, but the bedrock of their success has always been homegrown talent.

Along came COVID-19 followed by name, image and likeness – all of which threw recruiting cycles out of whack. Now comes the initiation of the 5-in-5 eligibility model.

“We used to write out on a whiteboard four or five seasons (rosters) and what that looks like,” assistant coach Craig Fortier said.

Gonzaga doesn’t do that anymore.

“What Lisa promotes is ‘Let’s bring in great people that can get better,’ ” Craig said. “And if we can keep them, then they will get better. We’re always going to be excited to have them as long as we can have them. We never want to have somebody that we’re kind of happy when they head out the door.”

Four of five starters on Gonzaga’s Super Seniors team in 2023-24 were prized high school recruits, developed over four or five years. Interestingly, though, it created some roster consternation. The last two recruiting classes have brought in four freshmen, one of whom transferred out this spring. The 2026-27 roster features one freshman. And the Zags have one commitment for the 2027 class.

How many more players Gonzaga will need to bring in next year depends on how many seniors exercise a fifth-year option created with the new eligibility format.

Seniors Taylor Smith, Zeryhia Aokuso and McKynnlie Dalan – each of whom transferred to Gonzaga – may opt to play another year, transfer for their final season or walk away from basketball.

This year’s roster features six juniors who could play three more seasons including this season. Junior Lauren Whittaker, who was listed on the roster as a redshirt freshman a year ago, is now listed as a junior to be in compliance with the new eligibility rule.

Seven of Gonzaga’s 13 players are transfers. No previous roster has had more transfers.

Thankfully most of Gonzaga’s transfers over the years have had at least two years of eligibility and in some cases three and maybe four.

Of the current group of transfers, Dalan could end up playing four at Gonzaga after spending her freshman season at the University of Minnesota. Former Mead three-sport standout Teryn Gardner could spend four years with the Zags.

Fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt, who hopes a temporary injunction granting her another year eligibility holds up this season, transferred from UConn to Gonzaga two years ago.

This year’s transfers – junior guards Emmy Roach (Rider) and Jocelyn Medina (Denver) – could spend three seasons at Gonzaga.

“So they’ve started to become our guys in our culture because we’ve had them for a while,” Craig Fortier said. “No matter if they’re a transfer or a freshman, the pattern is always going to be development. The more time you get with them, the better generally you’re gonna do. But we’re also trying to be effective and efficient with whatever amount of time we have with them in getting people up to speed with how we want to play and how we think we can help them be the best versions of themselves. That’s always evolving.”

Technically, the Zags have two scholarships available by NCAA rule. But Gonzaga has never had 15 on scholarship at one time.

Gonzaga has a commitment from Gonzaga Prep point guard Aylah Cornwall, who will sign during the early signing period in November. She will essentially fill Bettencourt’s scholarship.

Lisa Fortier says she and her staff continue to recruit for the class of 2027. That’s largely because it’s not known who will exercise a fifth-year option or perhaps transfer. Fortier always wants to have a scholarship in her back pocket.

“We aren’t done with (the 2027 class) yet,” Fortier said. “Most coaches right now are not just taking any high school kid. They have to be a really good fit or a really talented player.”

Gonzaga coaches have been out and about recruiting this fall. The Zags just offered AnnaClaire Bugbee, a 6-2 forward from Mandan, North Dakota, a position in the class of 2028. Bugbee posted a photo of herself with Gonzaga’s coaches on social media recently.

Fortier and her staff are recruiting players for 2028 and 2029.

“We’re recruiting all the time – it never stops,” Fortier said. “Our best players were high school recruits. They are homegrown. That’s a recruiting model we’re comfortable with. It’s hard to place a value on those program kids. You can point to programs like ours where you grow them up, take good care of them and you coach them well. And when they stay they’ll give everything. That’s the kind of people you want on your team – as many of them as you can.”

Gonzaga.title: Loaded Gonzaga women will be team to beat in rebuilt Pac-12
Gonzaga.summary:
The Gonzaga women’s basketball team should discover that many hands make lighter work this season.

Like 10 sets of hands – and maybe a couple more sets depending on the impact of transfers and a freshman.

All five starters return from a team that finished 24-10 and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

Truth is the Bulldogs have seven players capable of starting. And the other three will likely give coach Lisa Fortier pause when it comes to doling out playing time.

The Zags’ abundance of talent begins with 6-foot-3 forward Lauren Whittaker, who broke onto the scene last year as a redshirt freshman and was a force that West Coast Conference teams couldn’t contain. She was named the WCC Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year.

Whittaker is listed as a junior on this year’s roster. Gonzaga is being compliant with the NCAA’s new eligibility rules. Whittaker, who has exhausted a redshirt and used a medical waiver, can play three more years.

She led the Zags with 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game less than a year after having knee surgery. There’s no telling what Whittaker can do with a second year of strength added to her knee.

“It’s been so nice not to rehab anything,” Whittaker said. “I’ve gotten to work a lot on my fitness and stamina. I didn’t really get a summer workout session (last year) because I was just rehabbing the whole time.”

Floating on the perimeter and causing opponents frustration is junior guard Allie Turner, who will start for a third straight season.

An All-WCC first-team selection, Turner was the second-leading 3-point shooter in the nation last season and key to Gonzaga finishing as the top 3-point shooting team, a spot ahead of powerhouse UConn. Turner shot 47.1%, making 89 of 189. The Zags converted 39.2% (244 of 623).

Turner averaged 14.8 points, second best, and 3.5 assists per game.

It was thought Gonzaga would need to replace just one starter. But guard Ines Bettencourt, who graduated last spring, has been granted a fifth season through the NCAA’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model. Bettencourt and 70 other player plaintiffs in the California-based Glancey vs. NCAA lawsuit were granted a preliminary injunction by a California Superior Court judge. She’s still potentially awaiting final clearance from the courts.

A transfer from UConn, Bettencourt, one of Gonzaga’s best defensive players, averaged 6.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.1 assists per game.

Bettencourt became a strong voice among teammates last season. That should continue this season. She’ll get some assistance from Whittaker and Turner.

The Zags’ other two returning starters, seniors Taylor Smith (forward) and Zeryia Aokuso (guard), had flashes of brilliance last season. Smith should be much more effective and dangerous teaming with Whittaker in the high-low sets, and watch for Aokuso to play the point at times and create offense with her ability to get to the rim.

Forward Jaiden Haile, who was named the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year as a freshman last year, and junior guard Teryn Gardner played key roles off the bench. They would start for many teams, and don’t be surprised if either steps into a starting role at some point this year.

Senior forward McKynnlie Dalan, junior guard Christabel Osarobo and sophomore Julia Wilson round out the 10 returners. They will be fighting for minutes off the bench.

Joining the Zags are junior transfer guards Emmy Roach (Rider) and Jocelyn Medina (Denver) and freshman forward Abby Lusk, from Pocatello, Idaho. All three had solid minutes at FanFest.

“We have players who can make plays, who can make shots, who can rebound,” Fortier said. “We’re going to be able to play a lot of them and a lot of them are gonna be able to make an impact.”

With a team loaded with experience, preseason practices have allowed the Zags to pick up where they left off.

“We’re still gonna play with two forwards, we’re still gonna run the floor, we’re still gonna shoot a bunch of 3s,” Fortier said. “But within that context it does afford us an opportunity to wiggle a little bit and tinker.”

Gonzaga won’t have any difficulty scoring, and the Zags will look to push the pace whenever they can. But they must cut down on turnovers and improve defensively.

“Defensively we can be a lot better,” Turner said, pointing the finger squarely at herself.

The Zags were ranked 49th by Bart Torvik, whose analytical data is similar to the KenPom rankings in men’s basketball. No other non-Power Four school was represented in Torvik’s top 50.

Gonzaga is heavily favored to win the Pac-12 Conference in its first year in the rebuilt league.

It’s likely just the Pac-12 Tournament winner will earn a berth to the NCAA Tournament. The conference doesn’t have the credentials that the men’s teams have at this point.

The Zags don’t want to just get to the NCAA Tournament, though. They want to do something no other Gonzaga team has done – get to the Elite Eight, if not further.

“Win the conference tournament, make it to postseason and then hopefully get further than a game there this year,” Turner said.

Said Whittaker: “Everyone got a taste of what it’s like to be at the (NCAA) Tournament and everyone wants more. So it’s just elevating from what we had last year. We’ve built that foundation. No excuses. We’ve been together for a year.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga, even in new league, remain title favorites | Pac-12 women
Gonzaga.summary:
Pac-12 women’s basketball most likely will be divided into three tiers in the reconditioned conference.

Gonzaga and San Diego State should occupy the top two spots by season’s end.

Third through sixth – featuring Washington State, Colorado State, Oregon State and Boise State – will be highly competitive but could finish in any order.

And the three lowest places should be decided between Utah State, Fresno State and Texas State.

If Gonzaga plays as advertised, though, the Zags could make it a solo run to a conference championship, creating a fourth tier.

The Zags are expected to carry over their West Coast Conference dominance into the Pac-12.

Gonzaga is ranked No. 49 in the Bart Torvik preseason analytical data – the highest ranking for a non-Power Four conference school. Oregon State is 69th, Colorado State 80th and San Diego State 97th.

Here’s a look at the predicted order of finish:

1. Gonzaga. Easy, easy choice here.

None of the nine conference teams bring back a roster as deep as the Zags. Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who dominated in the WCC and was named the Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year last season, is expected to pick up where she left off. She’s the runaway pick as the Pac-12’s Player of the Year. Whittaker has plenty of support down low. Couple that with a perimeter that features the top 3-point shooting team in the nation a year ago and opponents will have to pick their poison in what they try to defend.

2. San Diego State. The Aztecs cruised to the Mountain West regular-season championship last year, stumbling once in 20 games. They were upset in the conference tournament, but extended their season in the WBIT where they were eliminated in the quarterfinals. SDSU has four of five starters back and add four transfers and three freshmen. The Aztecs finished 27-6 overall, tying the record for most wins in a season.

3. Oregon State. The Beavers can match up with any guards in the conference, but they sorely lack an experienced inside presence. OSU returns WCC All-Conference First Team picks Jenna Villa and Kennedie Shuler, both senior guards. Shuler was named the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and is arguably the best point guard in the conference. Villa, a transfer a year ago from Washington State, averaged 14.9 points in a breakout season.

4. Colorado State. The Rams won the MW Tournament last year, advancing to the NCAA Tournament where they showed well in a 65-62 loss to Michigan State and finished 27-8. CSU returns just one starter and bring in eight players including five transfers. The Rams have thrived in recent seasons on transfers.

5. Washington State. The Cougars have much to prove, but have a strong foundation. They return five starters – six if you count Malia Rudd, who started 20 games as a freshman. Leading the way is senior 5-8 guard Eleonora Villa, a second team All-WCC selection. The Italy native averaged a career-high 16.5 points and 3.6 assists while playing 34.8 minutes a game.

6. Boise State. The Broncos were highly competitive in the MW a year ago, finishing 25-9 overall and 14-6 in league. They must replace four starters. Coach Gordy Presnell begins his 39th season as a head coach, 21st at BSU. He’s six wins shy of 800 (794-392). The retooling will include three transfers and four freshmen.

7. Fresno State. The Bulldogs have much work ahead. They bring back one starter from a team that finished 15-18. The Bulldogs have brought in eight transfers and three freshmen. They get the nod here over Texas State based on playing in a tougher conference previously.

8. Texas State. The Bobcats have the lone new head coach in Chris Kielsmeier. He was previously a head coach at Cleveland State, Wayne State College and Howard Payne. Texas State brings back two starters. Kielsmeier signed eight transfers.

9. Utah State. The Aggies might as well be starting from rock bottom. They lost 18 straight to end last year after a 6-6 start. They return two starters, but wholesale changes are expected with six transfers.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga unanimously selected to win Pac-12 Conference in preseason media poll
Gonzaga.summary:
New league, same lofty expectations for a Gonzaga program that captured 27 regular-season championships and 23 conference tournament crowns during a 37-year residence in the West Coast Conference.

The Zags are expected to pick up right where they left off, selected as the unanimous favorite to win a Pac-12 Conference championship next spring by a panel of media members covering the league.

Gonzaga claimed each of the 17 first-place votes in the preseason poll released Thursday morning, just five days before Mark Few’s team opens the 2026-27 campaign with a juicy nonconference matchup against Matt Painter and Purdue.

Coming off its fourth straight NCAA Tournament appearance, Utah State was not surprisingly picked to finish second in the new conference, followed by No. 3 San Diego State, No. 4 Colorado State, No. 5 Oregon State, No. 6 Boise State, No. 7 Texas State, No. 8 Washington State and No. 9 Fresno State.

It continues a long run of preseason No. 1 nods for Gonzaga, which was picked to win the WCC every season since 2001, with the exception of the 2023-24 and 2017-18 seasons.

The 15th-ranked Zags were the only Pac-12 team to appear in the preseason Associated Press Top 25, but Utah State appeared on one AP ballot at No. 24, enough to earn two points in the poll.

Unlike other conferences, the Pac-12 did not release preseason all-conference teams, or announce a preseason player of the year, instead naming two players from each of the nine teams to the “2026-27 Men’s Basketball Impact List,” as selected by the league’s coaches.

Senior forward Braden Huff and sophomore wing Davis Fogle were Gonzaga’s selections – not unexpectedly, with both named to 20-player preseason watch lists for national positional awards this week. Fogle was named to the Julius Erving Award (small forward) watch list on Wednesday, one day before Huff was included on the watch list for the Karl Malone Award (power forward).

Huff had a 19-point, 11-rebound double-double in Gonzaga’s exhibition loss at Arkansas on Saturday and scored 11 points in 16 minutes during the team’s 91-59 victory over Lewis-Clark State. Fogle is just weeks removed from scoring 30 points in 20 minutes at Kraziness in the Kennel and had eight points against LCSC after missing the Arkansas exhibition with a left leg injury.

Washington State placed UNLV transfer Ladji Dembele and East Texas A&M transfer Ronnie Harrison on the Impact List. Harrison reached double figures in each of WSU’s two preseason exhibition games, scoring 23 points on 8 of 9 shooting in the Cougars’ 84-80 victory over cross-state rival Washington on Sunday.

Others named to the Impact List were Boise State’s Dovydas Butka and Damari Wheeler-Thomas, Colorado State’s Kyle Jorgensen and Jase Butler, Fresno State’s Bradey Henige and Ross Candelino, Oregon State’s Josiah Lake II and Daniel Freitag, San Diego State’s Elzie Harrington and Tae Simmons, Texas State’s Paul Djobet and DJ Hall, and Utah State’s Mason Falslev and Dallin Hall.

Gonzaga.title: Texas judge tentatively denies TRO for Chauncey Wiggins; Gonzaga wing remains ineligible before season opener
Gonzaga.summary:
A judge in McLennan County, Texas, has tentatively denied a temporary restraining order for Chauncey Wiggins and other player plaintiffs seeking a fifth year of eligibility, likely keeping the Gonzaga wing out of Monday’s season opener against Purdue in Las Vegas.

Wiggins and other athletes made a late push to join a lawsuit filed in Waco, Texas, against the NCAA after attempts to seek injunctive relief in other 5-in-5 lawsuits were unsuccessful.

The Gonzaga wing sought an alternate route to eligibility after a stay was granted in his Georgia lawsuit on Sept. 9. Wiggins and other players in the Georgia lawsuit, including Arizona forward RJ Godfrey and Boise State guard Lamar Washington, moved to withdraw their names from the case earlier this week and filed to join a group of athletes that previously received an injunction in the Wheeler v. NCAA case in Texas.

Presiding over the case, Judge Ryan Luna of the 414th Judicial District Court listened to arguments from both sides Thursday morning before tentatively denying the TRO for Wiggins and other plaintiffs applying for late inclusion.

At the end of a two-hour ruling, Luna granted an appearance for the group of players seeking inclusion in Wheeler v. NCAA, but denied a TRO for Wiggins and plaintiffs currently under stays in other state jurisdictions. Luna said he’d sign an order rejecting the TRO, “unless something in the briefing overwhelms me.” He gave the plaintiffs’ attorneys until 10 p.m. to file a briefing.

“Those players that you can identify that have already gone through this process on these merits, who have sought injunctive relief from another state court or granted it, I think we talked about Tennessee and Georgia,” Luna said. “Any of those players we can identify, I’m going to deny the TRO on those.”

It’s unclear what additional legal options exist for Wiggins, who could be on Gonzaga’s bench Monday afternoon while fellow 5-in-5 transfers Xaivian Lee (Florida) and Javon Bennett (Dayton) – currently eligible through legal decisions in California and Ohio – suit up against the Boilermakers in the season opener.

Godfrey committed to Arizona and former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd late in the offseason, but Thursday’s ruling means he also won’t be able to compete against UCLA in the second game of Monday’s doubleheader, which tips off at 7 p.m. in Vegas.

During Thursday’s hearing, Ryan Downton of Texas Trial Group, an attorney who’s representing a handful of athletes across the country in various 5-in-5 lawsuits, argued athletes would face irreparable harm if they weren’t able to obtain a fifth year of eligibility, citing the loss of scholarship, as well as name, image and likeness (NIL) and professional exposure.

“It does come down to the athletes and if the court believes the players are likely to prevail and suffer irreparable harm if they’re not permitted to play and there’s limited or no harm to the NCAA, if the court accepts the players should be here, the court should grant the injunction,” Downton said. “And the court should not penalize the players for availing themselves of their procedural rights any more than the NCAA should be punished to appeal decisions it doesn’t like.

“It ultimately comes down to the athletes. For any players before the court, is it equitable they play while this plays out, or is it equitable that they don’t?”

An NCAA attorney raised the issue of breach of contract, arguing any state’s law should govern the interpretation of that contract, and contending athletes from other lawsuits shouldn’t have the option to jump from one 5-in-5 case to the next.

“These plaintiffs are judicially estopped when coming in and saying that Texas substantive contract law should be applied to their contract claim, because they’ve already gone to Tennessee and Georgia to say substantive Tennessee and Georgia law applies to my breach of contract claim,” the NCAA attorney said. “So we can’t bring in Texas law here. … You’ve got to act in good faith, which would necessarily require you honor and respect the orders of other courts as opposed to just go somewhere else and say, ‘Well I didn’t really mean that Georgia and Tennessee law applies to my contract. I actually meant Texas was because that didn’t go the way I wanted it to.’ ”

Wiggins played three seasons at Clemson and one more at Florida State, averaging 13.3 points and 3.9 rebounds while making 38.7% from the 3-point line last year with the Seminoles. Before the fifth-year option was presented as a possibility, Wiggins joined the Boston Celtics at NBA Summer League, logging 8.3 minutes over three appearances in Las Vegas.

The 6-foot-11 wing made a pair of 3s and scored eight points during Gonzaga’s Kraziness in the Kennel scrimmage, but wasn’t eligible to suit up for the team’s exhibition games, on Saturday at Arkansas and Wednesday against NAIA Lewis-Clark State at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Bennett still eligible

Hours after Wiggins’ TRO was denied, Gonzaga got a positive update on the 5-in-5 eligibility front.

Bennett, one of three point guards that could see time in Few’s rotation this season, remains on track to play in Monday’s opener after the Ohio Supreme Court considered supplemental briefs from both parties in the Borovicanin v. NCAA lawsuit, keeping a previous ruling in effect.

Players in the case obtained a preliminary injunction in July, clearing them for a fifth season of eligibility, but a lower court issued a stay that temporarily overturned the original decision. A higher court then stayed that ruling earlier this month, reinstating the plaintiffs’ eligibility.

The Ohio Supreme Court examined the legality and the effect of an executive order issued on Oct. 13 by Ohio Governor Mike DeWine extending a fifth year of eligibility to athletes planning to compete at Ohio institutions in 2026-27. DeWine was sued by the NCAA in federal court, with the governing body arguing the decision would make it “impossible for all schools to compete on a level playing field.”

According to Thursday’s case announcement, “The order of the Hamilton County Common Please Court remains in effect pending this court’s consideration of the memorandum in support of jurisdiction.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Massamba Diop closes strong, Parker Jefferson impresses during LCSC exhibition | Rewind
Gonzaga.summary:
If Gonzaga fans didn’t overreact to a 76-72 loss at Arkansas on Saturday, it’s probably safe to apply the same approach to Wednesday’s 91-59 victory over NAIA Lewis-Clark State.

The 15th-ranked Zags got just about everything they wanted and needed from their final dress rehearsal and now look forward to Monday’s high-profile season opener against Purdue in Las Vegas.

What the Zags have in front of them is decidedly more exciting than what’s in the rearview mirror, but we’ll still take an opportunity to review three topics and storylines from Wednesday’s exhibition before moving on to Monday’s nationally televised opener at T-Mobile Arena.

Still processing

It’s been trial by fire for Massamba Diop through Gonzaga’s exhibition slate.

Gonzaga’s prized transfer portal pickup encountered foul trouble in both preseason games, was caught trying to trip Razorbacks forward Miika Muurinen in a sequence that resulted in technical fouls for both players and, above all else, is still adjusting to a new role in Mark Few’s system, with mixed results against Arkansas and LCSC.

The 7-foot-1 Diop conceded the opening tip to 6-foot-9 LCSC forward Dallon Morgan on Wednesday, but subsequently provided one of the game’s top highlights when he turned away Brandon Suber’s layup attempt three minutes into the opening frame, drawing a loud reaction from the home crowd.

Diop pulled down two defensive rebounds but committed his second and third fouls over a 15-second stretch that, in many ways, characterized his first two outings in a Gonzaga uniform.

After sitting the final eight minutes of the first half, Diop started in the second and made immediate contributions. The towering center scooped up an offensive rebound while picking himself up off the ground, maneuvered around L-C’s Dylan Skaife and jammed the ball into the basket.

“I think Massamba’s doing a decent job of protecting the basket for the most part right now, which is kind of what we haven’t had in a while,” Few said. “I think he needs to continue to keep working on rebounding and catching and finishing . The guards are finding him now. He’s playing with some good guards that can really manipulate ball screens and situations. He’s just got to slow down and catch the ball and finish. I think that’s kind of the next area of growth.”

Diop’s second-half turnaround was encouraging. The Arizona State transfer had eight of his 10 points after the break, finishing 5 of 7 from the field with five rebounds, one blocked shot and one steal.

“I think every day you see growth with him,” Braden Huff said. “It’s undeniable, his athleticism and length and his skill. Once we just get him to learn the system and what we need out of him, the sky is the limit for him. He’s going to be really good for us.”

Jefferson shines

Gonzaga picked up scoring and rebounding contributions from many of the usual suspects on Wednesday, but there were also a few surprises on the final stat sheet.

Parker Jefferson, for example, matched teammate Izan Almansa and LCSC’s Titus Yearout for a game-high 12 points on 6 of 9 shooting. Jefferson also led all players with six rebounds and two blocked shots to go with his two assists and one steal.

Jefferson enters the regular season as the fourth or fifth member of Gonzaga’s frontcourt rotation behind Huff, Diop, Almansa and potentially freshman center Sam Funches, but the sophomore forward has delivered in both of his exhibition stints, making 3 of 4 free throws at Arkansas with two rebounds and one steal in just under four minutes of action. Jefferson, whose mother Carrie played basketball at Arkansas and father Mike played for the Razorbacks’ offensive line, had a cheering section of nearly 40 family members and friends at Bud Walton Arena.

In Wednesday’s postgame presser, Gonzaga’s coach praised Jefferson for his connectivity, and not necessarily just on the court.

“Parker’s done a nice job. I’ll tell you what he’s done a really nice job of is helping us bring the team together,” Few said. “We didn’t have many returnees and he’s done a great job of welcoming everybody in and making them comfortable and just kind of being a great teammate, so obviously it’s nice to be able to reward him with some moments like that.”

More than ball

More than two months after destructive wildfires displaced thousands of Spokane residents, Gonzaga and LCSC agreed their preseason exhibition could be a good opportunity to raise funds for those rebuilding homes and replacing items lost from the blazes.

A portion of the money from ticket sales on Wednesday went toward Phase 2 of the Karen Worthy Memorial Grant, a nonprofit created to help those impacted by the Spokane Complex fires rebuild.

“I think this has been a really great opportunity for me to talk to the guys about, ‘Hey, these are people that are watching us on TV every game, these are people that are coming to our games, these are people that are wanting to meet you in the restaurants or see you walking around town,’ ” Few said. “I think it was really important that we kind of stepped up and again, kind of raised the awareness. Sometimes when you have events like this, everybody wants to run out and feels horrible about it and wants to give, but then as time goes on it starts waning and dissipating. I want us to kind of make another statement that hey, there’s still need out there right now.”

LCSC also chipped in to assist with the cause, donating its $5,000 game check to the Karen Worthy Grant. Warriors coach Austin Johnson had extended family members evacuated and one friend who lost his home as a result of fire damage.

“There’s tons of fees that aren’t really realized when you’re having to rebuild your whole house and home, or just anything that’s taken away with something like this,” Few said. “We’re happy to help and we’re hopeful because our guys are stepping up, myself and our guys are going to make a sizable dent in this. Hopefully other people will step up and follow along with us. Everybody, there’s still a huge, huge need and the insurances and all this doesn’t cover everything so that’s what we’re trying to do.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women picked to win new Pac-12; WSU selected sixth | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
With five starters and five other returners, it is no surprise that the Gonzaga women’s basketball team was tapped to win the Pac-12 Conference championship in a media poll released Thursday.

The Bulldogs’ top seven scorers return from a team that finished 24-10 and won the West Coast Conference title in its final season in the league.

Oregon State was picked to finish second in the remodeled conference. The Beavers may have been picked second based on their reputation and penchant for postseason success. In the final year of the original Pac-12 (2023-24), they advanced to the Elite Eight.

San Diego State, which won the Mountain West championship last year, was picked third followed by Colorado State, Boise State, Washington State, Fresno State, Texas State and Utah State.

Gonzaga received 16 of 19 first-place votes. Oregon State received one and San Diego State received two.

Colorado State won the MWC Tournament last year and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

WSU returns six players who started at various times. The Cougars have much to prove after stumbling to a 9-25 record last year.

ESPN released its preseason bracketology compiled by Charlie Creme on Monday. Gonzaga is picked as the automatic qualifier from the Pac-12 as a 10 seed. Oregon State and San Diego State are picked in the new 76-team field to play play-in games.

Players to watch

The Pac-12 also released its Preseason Impact List.

Gonzaga junior forward Lauren Whittaker, the WCC Player and Freshman of the Year last season, and junior guard Allie Turner, an All-WCC first-team selection a year ago, were two of 18 players named. Each school was allowed to nominate two players.

Named from WSU are seniors Alex Covill (post) and Eleonora Villa (guard), an All-WCC second-team pick last year.

Former WSU guard Jenna Villa and point guard Kennedie Shuler were selected from Oregon State. Shuler was the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and Villa was a first-team selection.

Add to the list

Gonzaga’s Whittaker was named to two more watch lists.

Whittaker, from Christchurch, New Zealand, is on the Naismith Trophy Women’s College Player of the Year preseason list along with the Katrina McClain Award preseason list. On Tuesday she was named to the Becky Hammon Mid-Major Player of the Year preseason list.

She is one of two Pac-12 players on the Hammon list.

In her first season playing for the Zags a year ago, Whittaker averaged 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game with 649 points and a school-record 348 rebounds.

Coach list

Lisa Fortier, who is entering her 13th season as head coach at Gonzaga, has been named to the Kathy Delaney-Smith Coach of the Year preseason watch list.

Fortier is one of 20 coaches nationally selected to the preseason list. The award is in its fourth season.

She enters the season four wins away from becoming the all-time winningest Gonzaga coach with a 313-84 overall record. That’s a .788 winning percentage. The winningest coach is Kelly Graves (316-136, .699), who is beginning his 13th season at Oregon.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga distributes 'meaningful minutes' to variety of players during 91-59 exhibition victory
Gonzaga.summary:
Mark Few would usually zero in on things like field goal percentage, rebounding or turnovers. With NAIA Lewis-Clark State visiting for Wednesday’s exhibition, Gonzaga’s coach was focused on another statistical column when judging whether the team’s final preseason tune-up was ultimately a success.

No, not final score. Gonzaga was expected to win in runaway fashion and had no issue, cruising past LCSC 91-59 at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Few’s eyes shifted to another section of the final stat sheet: minutes played. Everybody on Gonzaga’s roster registered at least four, with only one player, point guard Javon Bennett, exceeding 20 during Wednesday’s exhibition rout.

Another positive? The Zags left the Kennel without any injury concerns and should have everyone who played Wednesday available for Monday’s 4:30 p.m. (TNT/HBO Max) showdown with Purdue at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas.

“I think the best thing is we were able to get everybody in and get them kind of substantial minutes,” said Few, who wasn’t able to disperse playing time as liberally during a tightly contested exhibition loss at Arkansas on Saturday. “The other night, kind of the way it was going, you probably didn’t get as many guys in as you’d like, meaningful minutes. So getting everybody meaningful minutes tonight was probably the best thing.”

Scoring balance might have been a close second.

Gonzaga’s leading scorers, Parker Jefferson and Izan Almansa, both finished with 12 points but nine players had at least six. Joining Jefferson and Almansa in the double-digit club were Braden Huff and Bennett, who had 11 points apiece, along with Massamba Diop, who overcame a slow start to add 10.

Even in a dominant preseason win, though, Few was able to poke holes and identify shortcomings. The Zags were improved but still below-average from the perimeter, making 9 of 27 (33%) four days after a dismal 6 of 28 (214%) showing at Arkansas.

They won the rebounding column, but Few felt the 41-36 disparity should’ve been more substantial given the height, size and athleticism advantage Gonzaga still had over its NAIA opponent at nearly every position on the floor – even when Few’s reserves were in the game.

“Rebounding is something, we haven’t been good in the preseason here,” Few said. “Didn’t exactly do a great job tonight. We battled at Arkansas against a really good, big team but it’s something we’ve always got to take to heart because it’s going to be a big key to our season.”

Davis Fogle returned to Gonzaga’s starting lineup after taking precautionary measures and sitting out with a left leg injury against Arkansas. The sophomore wing played just 16 minutes, but was effective at both ends of the floor, scoring eight points on 4-of-9 shooting to go with two rebounds, two assists and two steals.

Gonzaga made its first two 3-pointers out of the gates, from starting guards Xaivian Lee and Isiah Harwell, and put together an impressive three-possession stretch minutes later when Diop blocked an LCSC shot into the first row, Harwell collected an offensive rebound before going back up for a dunk and Fogle converted on a steal-and-score sequence to extend a 7-0 run.

The Zags lost control of the game for a brief stretch after that, making a hockey substitution that saw the five starters replaced by five newcomers: Bennett, Nathan De Sousa, Luca Foster, Almansa and Sam Funches.

Fueled by seven straight points from Idaho transfer Titus Yearout, the Warriors went on an 8-0 run to close the deficit to 23-18 with 11 minutes, 11 seconds to play. But Gonzaga outscored its opponent 31-9 to close the frame and went into halftime with a 54-27 advantage.

Yearout led the Lewiston-based Warriors with 12 points, making 4 of 14 shots from the field and 2 of 6 from the 3-point line. Dylan Skaife, a Ferris High School product, scored five points on 2 of 7 from the field and 1 of 6 from the 3-point line.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga’s bench, led by Izan Almansa, contributes in exhibition blowout
Gonzaga.summary:
Izan Almansa received his eligibility just six days ago, but his intuitive play on the court makes it seem like he’s been in a Gonzaga uniform for a few years.

The 6-foot-10, 220-pound forward from Spain has been solid off the bench in a pair of exhibition games, including a 12-point effort in the first half of the Zags’ 91-59 exhibition rout over NAIA Lewis-Clark State College on Wednesday at the McCarthey Athletic Center.

The NCAA cleared Almansa on Friday, just before the team departed for Arkansas. One day later, Almansa was one of the most productive Zags, scoring 14 points in a 76-72 loss to 15th-ranked Arkansas in Fayetteville.

“It was right before the flight, coach (Stephen) Gentry told me,” Almansa said. “I wasn’t expecting to play. Everyone on the team got so hyped, me too. It was a really good moment.”

Almansa, who played for the NBA G League Ignite in 2023-24 and spent last season with Real Madrid in Spain’s Liga ACB, is on track to be the first big off the bench behind Braden Huff and Arizona State transfer Massamba Diop.

“He’s just got a very good feel for the game, so when you have that, everybody plays better with you and the game becomes a little easier for everybody,” head coach Mark Few said. “He knows when to pass, he understands spacing, he knows how to find his own shot.

“He’s just a really skilled basketball player. Those guys are always great to have on the floor from a coach’s perspective and also to play with.”

Almansa made 6 of 9 shots, including 1 of 2 3-pointers, against the talented Razorbacks. He hit 4 of 5 field-goal attempts, 2 of 2 on 3s, against LCSC.

“He’s obviously played against some really good players, some pros, in his time,” Huff said. “He’s super smart, athletic, quick. He’s a lot of fun to play with. I think he gives defenses a different look and he’s also really good on defense. He’ll be another big piece for us.”

Almansa was part of a GU bench that sputtered when five subs entered at the 14-minute mark of the first half. The Zags’ 11-point lead melted to seven before the starting unit returned.

The bench’s second run was a different story, outscoring the Warriors 18-2, boosting GU’s halftime lead to 54-27.

“Everyone was welcoming me great, knowing I wasn’t eligible at first,” said Almansa, whose first name is pronounced E-thun. “So it was a little bit hard, but everybody helped me, gave me a lot of confidence from my coaches, teammates, everybody here.”

Sophomore forward Parker Jefferson had nice stretches in each half and finished with 12 points, six rebounds, two assists and two blocks.

“I’m really proud of Parker,” said Huff, who scored 11 points in just 16 minutes. “He gave us good minutes (against Arkansas) and tonight he also did good things out there. I told him, I’ve been there coming off a redshirt year where you’re finally playing. I just told him to be ready regardless of what his role is night in and night out.”

Dayton transfer Javon Bennett, who had a tough shooting night (1 of 8) vs. Arkansas, chipped in 11 points, including three 3-pointers, and two assists against the visitors from Lewiston. Freshman guard Juwan Ekanga, a 6-6 freshman guard, added seven points, four rebounds and three assists. Gonzaga’s bench produced 47 points.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga's Chauncey Wiggins withdraws from Georgia 5-in-5 lawsuit, will pursue injunction in Texas
Gonzaga.summary:
Seeking expedited relief in his ongoing eligibility battle, Gonzaga transfer Chauncey Wiggins has withdrawn his name from a 5-in-5 lawsuit in the state of Georgia and will now pursue a legal injunction in Texas with the Bulldogs’ season opener just five days away.

Wiggins initially secured a fifth year of eligibility through a preliminary injunction in Georgia, but the NCAA subsequently filed for a stay that reversed the decision, making the former Florida State and Clemson player ineligible.

The Superior Court of Cobb County in Georgia recently set arguments for Jan. 12, 2027, which would’ve sidelined Wiggins through Gonzaga’s nonconference schedule as well as multiple Pac-12 Conference games, with no guarantee he’d receive an injunction.

Wiggins was one of 16 players who chose to withdraw from the case, according to a notice of voluntary dismissal without prejudice filed Tuesday by Cobb County Superior Court Clerk Henry Thompson. The group also includes RJ Godfrey, one of Wiggins’ former teammates at Clemson and someone expected to be a major contributor for former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd at Arizona, should he secure a fifth-year waiver.

Wiggins will continue to seek legal relief in another jurisdiction, applying to join a group of player plaintiffs in the Wheeler v. NCAA case taking place in McLennan County, Texas. Other player plaintiffs in the case – Baylor football player Hosea Wheeler, Texas Tech forward Darrion Williams, Utah State guard Dallin Hall and former Washington State guard Nate Calmese to name a few – were granted a preliminary injunction in September, clearing them to play until at least Dec. 14 when the case goes to trial.

An intervention hearing will take place at 7:30 a.m. on Thursday in Waco, Texas, to determine whether Wiggins and other members of the Godfrey v. NCAA will be added in the case and whether they’ll be eligible for the injunction that was extended to player plaintiffs in the original lawsuit.

The wing’s outside shooting would be a valuable weapon for Gonzaga if he’s cleared to play. Wiggins made a career-high 72 3s last season at Florida State, shooting at a 38.7% clip. He contributed to the 3-point shooting barrage at Kraziness in the Kennel, making 2 of his 5 attempts, but wasn’t eligible to suit up for Saturday’s exhibition at Arkansas, watching from the bench in a team sweatsuit as the Zags struggled from distance, finishing just 6 of 28.

Wiggins didn’t play in GU’s second exhibition on Wednesday against Lewis-Clark State, but fed passes to teammates during pregame warmups and was an active member of the bench during a comfortable win at McCarthey Athletic Center.

“He’s practicing every day and he’s been great,” Few said. “He’s been great, working out, looks good. Obviously would really help him when we hopefully do get him eligible here.”

In his lone season at Florida State, Wiggins averaged 13.3 points per game and 3.9 rebounds, shooting 47.9% from the field. He spent the three prior seasons at Clemson, starting in 43 of the 70 games as a sophomore and junior. Wiggins averaged 8.3 ppg during his junior season and 5.4 ppg as a sophomore.

Wiggins is one of three Zags who’ve taken legal action against the NCAA to secure a fifth year of eligibility. Xaivian Lee and Javon Bennett are eligible for the moment, but both still could face potential obstacles in lawsuits taking place in California and Ohio.
