Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga, LCSC made late push to schedule charity exhibition that will benefit Spokane wildfire victims
Gonzaga.summary:
With Gonzaga still in need of a second exhibition game last month, fourth-year assistant coach RJay Barsh made a familiar phone call right down the road.

Lewis-Clark State had always been game to make the two-hour trip north from Lewiston, visiting on three occasions under ninth-year coach Austin Johnson. It provides a unique opportunity for LCSC’s players to experience a top-15 college basketball heavyweight inside the Kennel and doubles as a chance for select members of Johnson’s roster to see friends and family in the Spokane area. For Gonzaga, it’s a solid tuneup against a competitive NAIA program that’s won 72% of its games under Johnson, a two-time NABC NAIA Coach of the Year.

Just one problem this year. The Warriors were completely booked. The NAIA has stringent scheduling limits and the Warriors didn’t have the flexibility to sneak another exhibition game onto their calendar.

Barsh had a potential solution, suggesting Gonzaga and Lewis-Clark State pitch the matchup as a charity exhibition that would raise money for Spokane wildfire victims. Johnson got to work on a petition that was submitted and subsequently approved by the NAIA.

The game is scheduled to tip off 6 p.m. Wednesday at McCarthey Athletic Center and will air locally on KHQ.

A generous and selfless gesture from LCSC’s coach followed. Johnson told Gonzaga to keep the $5,000 check the Warriors would receive from the exhibition and donate it to the Karen Worthy Memorial Wildfire Grant, a fund Bulldogs coach Mark Few helped launch to help families impacted by the Spokane Complex fires.

The amount isn’t insignificant to an NAIA program like LCSC – “a lot of money for us,” Johnson assured – but the Warriors’ coach had a personal connection to the wildfires and was happy to reroute the money to a good cause.

Johnson’s in-laws evacuated their Indian Trail home and watched numerous structures in their neighborhood disappear in the flames. Former LCSC forward Jared Tikker, an executive director of John Stockton’s Warehouse facility and the cousin of Johnson’s wife, Kelli, was forced to leave his home in Five Mile. Johnson’s close friend Jeremy Groth, the men’s basketball coach at Spokane Colleges, wasn’t as fortunate and lost his home in the fires.

“That’s one of the ways we’re getting the game is we promised the NAIA, we’re losing money, we’re spending money on gas and meals to go up there,” Johnson said. “We’re not making money. For me, it wasn’t just about getting the GU game, it was this can also be a good, positive thing.”

The objective for LCSC once the ball is tipped is the same as it was when the teams last played in 2024. No injuries, put together a few competitive stretches and give 40 minutes of effort, regardless of how lopsided the score gets.

“Last time we played them, we lost by 38, which that’s not something we do at LC State,” Johnson said. “So obviously you walk off the court and you feel like you are the worst team ever. I went back and looked and they have 14 or 15 wins by 38 or more since we played them. In retrospect, you look back and say maybe it isn’t that bad.”

LCSC has drawn the short stick over the years, often being the first opponent to get a glimpse of Gonzaga’s All-American frontcourt pairings before they’re introduced to the rest of the country in high-profile, nationally televised nonconference games.

Graham Ike and Braden Huff combined to score 45 points the last time the teams met in 2024, fueling the Zags to a 96-58 victory. Three years earlier, LCSC got an early preview of the Drew Timme-Chet Holmgren pairing that would help Gonzaga secure a top overall seed five months later at the NCAA Tournament. In 2019, Filip Petrusev and Anton Watson hurt the Warriors for 50 points in a 116-62 rout for the Zags.

On Wednesday night, LCSC will have to go through 7-1 Massamba Diop to score in the paint and deal with Huff’s polished post game when the Zags are on offense. Izan Almansa’s rebounding presents another issue off Few’s bench.

“Obviously they’re really good, because they haven’t asked us this year about what we’re going to do on ball screen coverage or this or that,” Johnson said. “So I don’t think I’m too worried about our X’s and O’s this year.”

Johnson knows his team can’t match up from a size or athleticism standpoint, but he’ll be encouraged if the Warriors manufacture 8-12 total minutes of “really, really competitive basketball.” He has fond memories of the trip in 2019. Well, the opening minutes of it. LCSC and Gonzaga were tied at 11-11 before Few switched to a pressing defense, sparking a 28-2 Bulldogs run.

“For us, we want to play hard,” Johnson said. “Not that Mark Few probably lays awake at night thinking about the LC State Warriors or anything like that, but I’d like to think one of the reasons we get asked back is we’re going to try to run some decent stuff. We want this to be good for them, too. I’d like to think we’ve been competitive enough to give them a look, but also they can try different rotations.”

LCSC’s Dylan Skaife, a junior who played under former GU forward Sean Mallon at Ferris High, is coming off an all-conference season with the Warriors. The sharpshooting guard, Johnson’s top returning scorer at 12.5 points per game, was the only Warrior to start in all 32 games last season and led the Cascade Conference in 3-pointers made with 90. That number also ranks fourth in a single season at LCSC.

“Can really shoot it, is our returning leading scorer, is off to a good start this year,” Johnson said. “I expect big things from him.”

Gonzaga.title: For No. 11 Gonzaga, clearance from the courts looms large | Wilner's Preseason Top 25
Gonzaga.summary:
Projecting the fate of basketball teams across the Division I landscape, extraordinarily difficult in the transfer portal era, is more challenging by an order of magnitude this fall because of unresolved eligibility lawsuits.

Hours before the 2026-27 season openers, the coaches don’t even know who’s playing and who’s sitting in the aftermath of the NCAA’s controversial 5-in-5 ruling in the spring.

“We have a court system in the U.S. and that’s going to impact our game this year,” Arizona coach Tommy Lloyd said last week at the Big 12’s preseason media event. “You just wish cooler heads would prevail, and give these kids the opportunity they deserve.”

Well, sure, but college basketball has never been a place for cool heads, logical decisions and thoughtful strategy.

As a result, we’re left to guess at the roster composition for myriad preseason favorites that are awaiting final decisions from the courts.

Alas, onward and upward.

Here’s my preseason Associated Press ballot (with comments added):

1. Florida: An easy call given the loaded list of returnees and coach Todd Golden’s deft touch. The frontcourt is sublime with Alex Condon, Thomas Haugh and Rueben Chinyelu, and the backcourt should be one of the best in the SEC. If they stay healthy, the 2025 national champs could make it two titles in three years.

2. Illinois: Despite the departure of star point guard Keaton Wagler, the Illini were not one-hit wonders with their run to the Final Four. Guard Andrej Stojakovic and forward David Mirkovic lead a veteran core that adds Providence transfer Stefan Vaaks.

3. Duke: Proven playmakers, elite recruits and one superstar transfer, John Blackwell (from Wisconsin), form what should be another title contender for coach Jon Scheyer. (Editor’s note: These rankings are specific to the regular season and not based on teams finding new and preposterous ways to blow leads in the NCAA Tournament.)

4. UConn: Yes, the Huskies were hit hard by attrition with the departures of Tarris Reed and Alex Karaban and with Solo Ball taking a medical redshirt. But the most important piece is back: coach Dan Hurley. Add guards Silas Demary and Braylon Mullins and we’re quite confident the sum will exceed the parts.

5. Tennessee: With an elite transfer class that includes VCU’s Terrence Hill, Wake Forest’s Juke Harris and Notre Dame’s Jalen Haralson – it might be the best in the land – the Volunteers are set for another commendable but fruitless attempt to become a basketball school.

6. Michigan State: The return of star guard Jeremy Fears cemented Michigan State’s status as a Big Ten favorite alongside Illinois. Whether the Spartans return to the Final Four for the first time since 2019 depends on the production level from everyone else.

7. Arizona: The Wildcats might have the best frontline west of Gainesville, Florida, with Ivan Kharchenkov, Motiejus Krivas and RJ Godfrey, the Clemson transfer whose eligibility remains uncertain. But for the Wildcats to replicate their 2025-26 success, the unproven backcourt must blossom – and Arizona won’t have Jaden Bradley to light the path.

8. Louisville: The Cardinals possess the No. 2-ranked transfer class in the country (behind St. John’s) with Oregon point guard Jackson Shelstad, Kansas big man Flory Bidunga, Arkansas wing Karter Knox and Iowa forward Alvaro Folgueiras. If Seth Trimble (North Carolina) remains eligible, coach Pat Kelsey will have everything needed for a deep run in March.

9. Arkansas: As usual, coach John Calipari landed a stellar freshman class with four five-star prospects, including the No. 1 wing in the country, Jordan Smith. But anyone who watched the Razorbacks last season knows defense was not a priority. Unless that changes, the Hogs won’t reach their lofty potential.

10. Texas: Could this be the year Sean Miller finally reaches the Final Four? His incoming class of recruits and transfers is one of the best in the land with guards Isaiah Johnson (Colorado) and Mikey Lewis (Saint Mary’s) and forward David Punch (TCU). If the Longhorns are healthy, there are no excuses.

11. Gonzaga: With Davis Fogle, Braden Huff and Massamba Diop, the Zags possess a frontline that compares favorably to those at Arizona and Florida. The backcourt? Who knows. Coach Mark Few has several gifted players awaiting clearance from the court system. If the legal outcomes are unfriendly, the journey through the rebuilt Pac-12 could prove arduous.

12. St. John’s: Another school with major unresolved eligibility issues, although Baylor transfer Tounde Yessoufou is set to play and could have a massive impact. And unlike the other 364 schools in Division I, the Red Storm have Rick Pitino.

13. USC: This placement is based, in part, on Eric Musselman being a Year 3 coach. He led Nevada to the Sweet 16 in his third season in Reno and Arkansas to the Elite Eight in his third season in Fayetteville. Everything is set for success with returnees Rodney Rice, Alijah Arenas and Jacob Cofie, plus blue-chip recruits and a solid collection of transfers.

14. Houston: This is the first time the Cougars have not appeared in the Hotline’s preseason top 10 since we-can’t-remember-when. Joseph Tugler’s return should spur the harrowing defense, but the offense must be rebuilt around point guard Dedan Thomas, who averaged 15 points for LSU, and returning wings Mercy Miller and Chase McCarty.

15. Vanderbilt: Point guard Tyler Tanner’s decision to withdraw from the NBA draft at the deadline was one of the most significant in the country, offering the Commodores a chance to remain relevant. The transfer class features high-scoring former Washington State guard Ace Glass.

16. Nebraska: Many of the low-profile players who led the Cornhuskers to their greatest season are returning, with leading scorer Pryce Sandfort atop that list. But how will everyone associated with the program manage the expectations that are present in Lincoln for the first time in forever?

17. Alabama: Coach Nate Oats has proven adept at assimilating disparate parts rapidly. Combine returnee Aden Holloway with uber-recruit Jaxson Richardson and transfer Drew Fielder (Boise State), and the Crimson Tide has a core that can flourish.

18. Miami: The momentum continues for second-year coach Jai Lucas, who led the Hurricanes to 26 wins in his rookie year and landed two top transfers in Georgia center Somto Cyril and Villanova guard Acaden Lewis.

19. Virginia: The Cavaliers possess the NIL game necessary to compete for elite talent and a top-tier position in the ACC. Leading scorer Thijs De Ridder is returning. Add UC Irvine transfer Jurian Dixon, and coach Ryan Odom has a conference title contender.

20. Michigan: Coach Dusty May’s departure to the NBA was one of several offseason gut punches the 2026 national champions were forced to absorb. They also lost star recruit Brandon McCoy to a season-ending injury. Defending a title is never easy. In Michigan’s case, it will be brutally difficult.

21. Kansas: The decision to accept Purdue transfer Trey Kaufman-Renn, who was drafted and played in the NBA summer league, was deplorable. His eligibility isn’t guaranteed. The basketball gods will render judgment, and it won’t be pleasant for the Jayhawks. Not for nothing: Although Kaufman-Renn’s return doesn’t technically violate Big 12 rules, it violates the spirit of the August decision to ban professionals.

22. Saint Louis: Most of the key pieces to coach Josh Schertz’s 29-win machine are back. (So, too, is Schertz.) St. John’s and Gonzaga should be the best of the non-football schools next season, with the Billikens No. 3.

23. North Carolina: Michael Malone is a first-rate coach whose adjustment to the college game could take two months. That leaves three for the Tar Heels to excel.

24. Iowa: There’s a case for Ben McCollum as the top NCAA Tournament coach in the sport not named Dan Hurley, but these rankings are based on the regular season. And without court maestro Bennett Stirtz, the Hawkeyes might encounter a few potholes.

25. VCU: The Atlantic 10 could be the best of the midmajor conferences with VCU and Saint Louis leading the charge to relevance.

Also considered: BYU, Indiana, Iowa State, Kentucky, Miami (Ohio), Missouri, New Mexico, Ohio State, Purdue, San Diego State, Santa Clara, Syracuse, TCU, Texas A&M, Texas Tech, UCLA, Utah State, Villanova and Wisconsin

Send suggestions, comments and tips (confidentiality guaranteed) to wilnerhotline@bayareanewsgroup.com or call 408-920-5716

Gonzaga.title: Five former Gonzaga players named to NBA G League rosters for 2026-27 season
Gonzaga.summary:
Twelve former Gonzaga players appeared on NBA opening day rosters and five more could be one call away as they open the 2026-27 season in the NBA’s G League.

Two members of last year’s Gonzaga team, Jalen Warley and Tyon Grant-Foster, will start their professional careers in the G League, along with another trio of former Bulldogs that includes Anton Watson, Nolan Hickman and David Stockton.

Warley signed with the Indiana Pacers’ G League affiliate, the Noblesville Boom, after agreeing to join the Eastern Conference franchise at NBA Summer League in Las Vegas, where he impressed coaches and front office personnel with his defensive play and versatility.

Grant-Foster didn’t stick with the San Antonio Spurs after a Summer League assignment, but managed to sign on with the Miami Heat’s G League squad, the Sioux Falls Skyforce, after being selected No. 15 overall during Saturday’s G League draft.

Entering his third professional season since leaving GU, Watson, a Gonzaga Prep product, is returning to the Los Angeles’ Lakers G League affiliate but will be playing home games in a different arena after the team switched from South Bay, playing in El Segundo, to Coachella Valley in Palm Desert.

Watson was one of South Bay’s top performers last year, averaging 11.3 points, 5.0 rebounds, 3.0 assists and 1.3 steals over 36 games and 24 starts.

Hickman is returning to the Capital City Go-Go (Washington Wizards) for the second season since going undrafted in 2025. The former Gonzaga guard was a part-time starter for Capital City last season, starting in 17 of 33 games, and averaged 10.8 ppg and 3.6 apg while shooting 43% from the field and 39.5% from the 3-point line.

Stockton, who recently agreed to a deal with the Valley Suns (Phoenix Suns), is back for his sixth stint in the G League after spending a year with Piratas de Quebradillas of the Baloncesto Superior Nacional in Puerto Rico. The former GU point guard and son of Gonzaga legend John Stockton played for the Valley Suns in 2024-25 and could share the court this season with Drew Timme, who’s on a two-way deal with Phoenix.

Timme is one of four ex-Zags who could split their time between the NBA and G League this season. Graham Ike (Golden State Warriors), Ryan Nembhard (Denver Nuggets) and Malachi Smith (Toronto Raptors) also entered the 2026-27 campaign on two-way contracts.

Guard Hunter Sallis, who played two seasons at Gonzaga before transferring to Wake Forest returns to the G League San Diego Clippers (Los Angeles Clippers), while wing Michael Ajayi, who spent a season in Spokane between stops at Pepperdine and Butler, is on a two-way deal with the Charlotte Hornets after going undrafted in June.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women see plenty of bright spots in exhibition rout of Westmont
Gonzaga.summary:
As exhibitions go, it was true to form.

Dig deeper and it’s clear to see why there’s excitement about two teams that play in McCarthey Athletic Center.

Nearly a month to the day of its first preseason practice, the Gonzaga women’s basketball team showed it was ready to play Tuesday, cruising past the NCAA Division II Westmont College Warriors 84-43 before 4,490.

All 12 available Gonzaga players saw time in the first half, and a freshman made an emphatic debut.

Abby Lusk, the Zags’ lone freshman from Pocatello, Idaho, made the first two shots of her career, both 3-pointers, and had 10 points on 4 of 4 shooting in five minutes.

Impressive considering she had been out a week after spraining an ankle. Coach Lisa Fortier said Lusk was a game-time decision.

“It’s the little things that, like, Little Me dreamed about,” Lusk said of her debut. “Getting your first college baskets. It’s just a surreal moment. Being able to make two (back-to-back 3-pointers) is kind of fun too. Seeing the love and support from the bench and the girls on the court … it was everything I envisioned it being.”

Lusk finished with 12 points and four rebounds in 11 minutes.

“We wanted to get her under the lights and see how she did,” Fortier said. “And she did very well. … I think her parents would have come up if they would have known she was going to play. But we had no idea.”

Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who was the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season, scored Gonzaga’s first basket. Whittaker ate up the smaller Warriors inside in the opening 20 minutes with 16 points on 6-of-8 shooting to go with four rebounds, two assists and two steals. She finished with a game-high 24 points, six rebounds and three assists in 21 minutes.

Four of five starters from a year ago started Tuesday and Mead High graduate and junior guard Teryn Gardner stepped into the lineup, replacing fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt.

The lone Zag not to play was sophomore forward Jaiden Haile, who was the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year last season. She was wearing a boot from an overuse injury. She started shooting in light practice last week.

Every Gonzaga player logged at least 10 minutes.

Another bright spot was the play of senior guard Zeryhia Aokuso. She scored from all areas, finishing with 14 points in 18 minutes.

Gonzaga asserted authority early in the third quarter, using a 7-0 spurt to set the tone. It was the most pleasing stretch for Fortier.

“The thing I liked the most was how we came out in the third,” Fortier said. “Hopefully our team is going to be a team that gets leads and then play from the front versus always coming from behind. We talked at halftime about what our energy was going to look like in the third. I thought it was really good energy, probably our best quarter.”

It was the second game in two days for Westmont, from Santa Barbara, California. The Warriors fell 71-46 at Washington State on Sunday.

Gonzaga opens the season with three straight home games, beginning Monday when North Dakota State visits. The Bison are picked to win the Summit League championship.

NDSU is similar to Gonzaga. The Bison return four of five starters including a Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year.

Gonzaga opened the season at NDSU last year, winning 81-66.

“North Dakota State is really good,” Fortier said. “So it’s a tough opener. Hopefully we’ll get the best work we can in the next few days.”

Gonzaga.title: No. 12 Arkansas Holds Off No. 15 Gonzaga in Exhibition
Gonzaga.summary: FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. – In an exhibition matchup between Top 15 teams, No. 12 Arkansas rallied to defeat No. 15 Gonzaga, 76-72, Saturday inside Bud Walton Arena.

Gonzaga.title: Despite loss, No. 15 Gonzaga finds value in 'high-level' exhibition meeting with No. 12 Arkansas | Rewind
Gonzaga.summary:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ark . – Two hours before tipoff, a line of students started to form outside Bud Walton Arena, snaking through a grass courtyard and stretching out to a block of academic buildings 30 to 40 yards away.

Later on, a security guard led Arkansas’ iconic “Woo Pig Suie” chant, drawing a positive response from the few hundred students waiting to get in the door.

With an announced attendance of 16,436, Saturday’s meeting between No. 12 Arkansas and No. 15 Gonzaga was an exhibition in name only. If that wasn’t evident beforehand, it became clear once the ball was tipped, with six lead changes, physical play at both ends and a brief dustup between Gonzaga’s Massamba Diop and Arkansas’ Miika Muurinen that resulted in double technical fouls.

Arkansas won 76-72, but Gonzaga didn’t come away empty-handed from the experience.

“This was a great experience for us and great to see what Cal’s built here,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said of longtime friend and Arkansas counterpart John Calipari. “It was great seeing Fayetteville. Really, really impressed with the whole area and all that, so we’ll take what we can and we’ll learn from this. All in all, I’m pretty happy for everything.”

Our first exhibition rewind of the 2026-27 season takes a deeper look at the relationship between the Naismith Hall of Fame coaches, eligibility news Gonzaga received roughly 24 hours before tipoff in Fayetteville and the Bulldogs’ point guard situation.

Mad respect

The Few-Calipari relationship can be traced back to the early 2000s, when both coaches were trying to get quality games on their nonconference schedules while at Gonzaga and Memphis.

“You may say, how did you two get together?” Calipari said. “Both of our programs needed each other. I was at Memphis, he was at Gonzaga just getting it going and we needed each other. When we started playing, I wouldn’t play him at the pound (Kennel) because it’s 8,000, 9,000 and it’s crazy students. So I said I’ll play you in Spokane. It was huge television, it helped both programs and he and I have stayed close since then.”

Calipari regrettably agreed to a six-year nonconference series with Gonzaga, traveling to Numerica Veterans Arena in 2022-23 and hosting Few’s team at Rupp Arena the following season. Gonzaga won the first meeting convincingly, 88-72, and squeaked by Kentucky the following season, 90-89, for an important resume-boosting win that put Few’s team on the right side of the NCAA bubble.

“And me being goofy, I’m at Kentucky now, let’s play,” Calipari said. “We go to his place, they beat us by like 20 – I think they were up by 30 at halftime. Then they come to our place, how hard is it to win in that building? Well, they won and they won by about 30 last year and I think they canceled the series. But Mark’s terrific and you notice they never gave up.”

Saturday’s exhibition can be mutually beneficial for Gonzaga and Arkansas teams that boast preseason top-15 rankings and both have Final Four aspirations. The coaches plan to debrief in the coming days to share thoughts and notes about their teams, hoping to gather valuable intel that can help one week out from the regular season.

“Anytime we get our teams together, it’s always a high-level game,” Few said. “We have teams that can compete for Final Fours and obviously can play deep into the tournament. So it’s fun in that way. In an exhibition game, it’s fun to play against your friends. It’s not playing against your friends in real games, it’s kind of torturous. But yeah, we’ve had quite a year together here.”

Few and Calipari have had more run-ins than usual the last three months.

The Arkansas coach was one of three active Naismith Hall of Famers – along with Grant Hill and John Stockton – to present Few when he received his orange jacket in Springfield, Massachussetts, two months ago.

The coaches met up again at Capitol Hill in Washington , D.C. , last month to advocate for the Protect College Sports Act that would institute sweeping changes across college sports, including a cap on revenue sharing and new transfer regulations.

The bill likely came up in conversation when Few, Calipari and Gonzaga athletic trainer Josh Therrien met for dinner Friday night at Cheers, a Southern comfort restaurant in downtown Fayetteville.

“I just think when you have a bipartisan bill that passed the Senate 78-22, name the last bill that passed the Senate 78-22,” Calipari said. “We’ve got to get it through the house. I’ve made it clear, I’m being selfish. I’ve got a son in this, Mark has a son in this, Tom Izzo has a son in this, Kelvin Sampson has a son in this. We’ve all got sons in this, you want to leave it this way?”

Almansa’s arrival

Gonzaga teammates describe Izan Almansa as stoic and even-keeled – someone who doesn’t express much emotion when he’s on the court and probably even less he’s away from it. But even Almansa couldn’t hide his grin when the Spanish forward learned he was cleared by the NCAA on Friday morning, just before Gonzaga boarded its charter flight to Fayetteville.

“He’s a dude who’s pretty quiet,” Braden Huff said, “but you could see the excitement on his face when he got the news and we were all super excited for him.”

It marked the end of a five-month wait for Almansa, who committed to Gonzaga in May but faced a long, uncertain road to eligibility given his professional experience overseas and tenure in the NBA G League. Almansa most recently played at Real Madrid in the Spanish ACB, but also had yearlong stints with the Perth Wildcats of Australia’s NBL and G League Ignite.

Almansa, who hadn’t been part of Gonzaga’s exhibition plans even 30 hours earlier, was Few’s top contributor off the bench and played valuable minutes spelling Diop when the 7-foot-1 center encountered foul trouble in the first half.

The sophomore was GU’s second-leading scorer behind Huff, totaling 12 points on 6 of 9 from the field and 1 of 2 from the 3-point line. He also had six rebounds and led the Zags with two blocked shots.

“That’s a big get for us, he was huge today,” Huff said. “I expect that from him all season. For him to be eligible is great, he’s going to be really good for us.”

Point of concern?

Even with three point guards in place now, the position group that dominated offseason headlines continues to be something to monitor closely eight days out from the season opener against Purdue.

Xaivian Lee, Nathan De Sousa and Javon Bennett all had stints on the ball Saturday, with De Sousa getting the largest share of minutes (33), followed by Lee (19) and Bennett (16).

Provided he stays eligible through an injunction in his California lawsuit, Lee is expected to handle starting point guard duties, though foul trouble limited his opportunities in Saturday’s exhibition. The Florida transfer navigated early shooting struggles to make two momentum-shifting 3-pointers late in the game and finish with eight points on 3 of 6 shooting and 2 of 4 from distance.

It was a rough go for De Sousa in his first collegiate game. The French native posted horrendous shooting numbers, making 2 of 17 shots from the field and 1 of 8 from the 3-point line, but he had three assists with just one turnover and tied for the team lead with two steals.

“They struggled, they struggled to shoot the ball,” Few said. “But Nate’s got quite the fighting spirit. He’s a tough guy, we knew that. I’d say Xaivian did a nice job of responding there, especially in that second run, we put him in to step up and make shots because he was struggling a bit early and he got the fouls.”

According to Few, Bennett learned he’d be eligible to play in Saturday’s exhibition not long before tipoff. Similar to Lee, the fifth-year senior is currently involved in a 5-in-5 lawsuit and recently got a favorable decision from the Ohio Supreme Court, which issued a stay to temporarily clear player plaintiffs listed in the case.

Few partially attributed Bennett’s offensive struggles on Saturday to . The Dayton transfer was 1 of 8 from the field and 0 of 4 from the 3-point line, scoring only two points.

“Javon will be fine, he knows how to make buckets and get in there,” Few said. “He got the news very, very late today, right before the game that he was going to be eligible to play. I’m not sure as far as preparation may be, I think that may have impacted him a little bit. They definitely have room for improvement after looking at those numbers right there.”

Gonzaga.title: Davis Fogle-less Gonzaga struggles offensively, falls 76-72 to Arkansas in exhibition
Gonzaga.summary:
FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. – College basketball exhibition games often come with an extended list of asterisks. The list for Saturday’s preseason matchup between No. 12 Arkansas and No. 15 Gonzaga ran slightly longer than normal.

The Razorbacks prevailed 76-72 over the Zags in a back-and-forth game that featured at least three major momentum swings and saw both teams lead by as many as 10 points.

As for the asterisk, or caveat, even Arkansas coach John Calipari couldn’t avoid pointing out on multiple occasions during a postgame press conference? Davis Fogle was parked at the end of Gonzaga’s bench in street clothes, not stuffing the stat sheet for a team that went through multiple dry spells offensively in both the first and second half and didn’t make a 3-pointer for the first 15 minutes.

“Their best player wasn’t playing,” Calipari told reporters, “so this probably would’ve been a different game.”

If the point wasn’t clear enough, Calipari came back around to it later on in a 14-minute postgame availability, stressing how much of a difference Fogle could’ve made had he been on the floor, not resting an injured left leg at Bud Walton Arena.

“Let me say this, too. That team over there with Fogle, I told Mark (Few) after, I grabbed him I said, ‘You play Fogle, we get beat by 20 today,’” Calipari said. “Because he’s another veteran, shooting 3’s, off the bounce, the kid’s a pro. And he didn’t play today. He’s okay, but (Few) said, ‘He just banged up his knee and I’m going to leave him out, it’s an exhibition game.’ And their first game is a hard game. But they’re good.”

Fogle or no Fogle, the Zags also have plenty of room for growth – a reality for virtually all 365 Division I basketball teams in the country during the final week of October.

Despite missing its first 11 looks from the 3-point line, Gonzaga managed to take an early lead and stayed in front for the majority of the first half, going up by double digits on Braden Huff’s jumper with 2 minutes, 14 seconds to play.

Arkansas responded with an offensive storm that stretched from the final stages of the first half to the opening minutes of the second. All told, it was an 18-0 Razorbacks run – a 9-0 run in the first half followed by an identical 9-0 run in the second – that ultimately helped Calipari’s team go up 50-39 on Cooper Bowser’s dunk with 14 minutes, 21 seconds to play.

The contributing factors to Arkansas’ game-turning run?

“Really bad offense by us,” Few said. “But obviously, it was impacted and caused by great defense by Arkansas. I think that was a major thing and that was a stretch where somehow we ended up on the positive side of the rebounds and second-chance points, but it sure didn’t feel like that. Definitely not during that stretch right there.

“Also those free-throw rebounds, it was crazy. I think they just got eight to 10 points on free throw rebounds and block outs.”

The Zags still weathered the storm and had chances down the stretch to tie the game or go back in front. Huff got a short floater to rattle in with 2 minutes, 17 seconds left, trimming Gonzaga’s deficit to five points, and Xaivian Lee knocked down a pull-up 3-point shot in transition to make it 68-66. After Miika Muurinen’s layup stretched the lead back out to four points, Huff came back down and got another floater to fall.

But Arkansas freshman Davion Thompson responded with a clutch pull-up 3-pointer from the top of the arc and Gonzaga trailed by two possessions for most of the final minute, until Izan Almansa converted a tip-in with four seconds to play.

There were plenty of teaching points for a Gonzaga team that finished 6 of 28 (21.4%) from the 3-point line weeks after making 18 of 33 at Kraziness in the Kennel. The Zags often struggled to defend without fouling and four players finished with four fouls apiece. The Razorbacks went to the charity stripe for 30 free throws, but made just 17.

“That’s what these games are great for,” Few said. “I thought it was an awesome, awesome environment. In the past, we’ve done closed-door scrimmages and stuff and there’s a lot to be gained from that. But this was a great experience for us.”

Huff shrugged off a slow shooting start to finish with game-highs of 19 points and 11 rebounds. Spanish forward Izan Almansa was Gonzaga’s only other double-digit scorer, scoring 14 points and pulling down six rebounds roughly 30 hours after he was deemed eligible by the NCAA.

Billy Richmond III led the Razorbacks with 17 points while Thompson had 12 and both Muurinen and JJ Andrews finished with 10 apiece.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women show off versatility, experience during Fan Fest scrimmage
Gonzaga.summary:
Most Fan Fest’s are a happy-go-lucky time, nothing more than an opportunity to put the jersey on for the first time and take to the court under the lights.

For the Gonzaga women’s basketball team, Saturday was different. The Zags didn’t just want to go through the motions. Ten of them played in the Fan Fest a year ago and they weren’t happy with the product they put on display.

Yes, the Zags were squaring off against their teammates, their friends. But judging by the competitiveness, it meant something to them.

Few will remember the score or which color prevailed come March. But for the record, Blue, led by Lauren Whittaker, Ines Bettencourt and Teryn Gardner, topped White 42-30 in the 20-minute scrimmage at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Equivalent to half a game, Whittaker, the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season had 12 points, five rebounds, two assists and two steals. Bettencourt, who is seeking a fifth year of eligibility and is presently eligible, had 10 points and Gardner, who is vying for a starting position and more playing time this season, had nine points on 3-of-6 shooting from 3-point range.

Gonzaga was the top 3-point shooting team in the nation, and the Zags will likely be among the leaders again this season. Blue and White combined to make 9 of 18 from distance.

But as the scrimmage showed, the Zags can do a number of things. And there’s much room for improvement. Coach Lisa Fortier, who along with dedicated assistants Stacy Clinesmith, Jordan Green and husband, Craig Fortier, begin their 13th season, will watch the Fan Fest video.

“We’ll go back and see all the problem areas,” Fortier said. “Half the time I was talking to my friends (during the scrimmage). So we’ll definitely go back and watch (the video).”

As she always does at Fan Fest, Fortier left the in-game coaching to her assistants.

“I liked how we were trying to push the ball (in transition), get the ball outletted faster, run the floor harder,” Fortier said. “We’ve done it in a little bit different way in the past where we’ve had the point guard really pass it full court. So last year we got bogged down a little bit with too many dribbles in transition. So I thought our team ran hard and looked to (pass) the ball to people. We didn’t always score in transition, but we’re getting those opportunities.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile sat out, her left foot still in a boot recovering from what she called an overuse injury. She said she expects to be back in two to three weeks.

Eleven of 12 Zags scored. Interestingly, the one who didn’t, junior guard Allie Turner, won the 3-point shooting contest. She edged Gardner. Turner and Gardner led the Zags in 3-point shooting last year.

All three new Zags - freshman Abby Lusk and transfers Emmy Roach and Jocelyn Medina - scored. Roach led with six points.

Bettencourt had an interesting passing partner during the 3-point shooting contest - former UConn teammate Azzi Fudd, the No. 1 draft pick by the Dallas Wings in the 2025 WNBA draft.

All five returning starters made cases for securing their starting job. And Gardner is certainly making a case to be a starter.

“There are people who are more likely (to start) based on their tenure here,” Fortier said. “Last year we ended up starting the same lineup (every game). That’s kind of been our style, but we’re always trying to not have that be a thing. You have to earn it every day in practice and even after you’ve gotten it that doesn’t mean you get it forever.”

Bettencourt thought the Zags did a number of things well Saturday.

“I mean, what is there not to like,” Bettencourt said. “We started off strong with our (drill) competitions - what we can do individually and then in the scrimmage. We were just having fun. It’s always better to be playing in front of a crowd instead of a silent gym and the coaches yelling at us constantly. It was just good to be back in front of the fans.”

That’s why they call it Fan Fest.

Gonzaga.title: Loaded with experience, Gonzaga women appear better than ever ahead of annual Fan Fest
Gonzaga.summary:
When it comes to the Gonzaga women’s basketball team’s Fan Fest, it’s less about execution and more about embracing the moment.

More than anything, it’s the first opportunity for the Zags to wear their uniforms and step onto the court at McCarthey Athletic Center in a pseudo-competitive environment. Just because the Bulldogs aren’t playing a real opponent, playing against each other can bring out the competitive spirit.

After all, teammates don’t like to lose to teammates – whether it’s a table-top game, a 3-point shooting contest or an intrasquad scrimmage.

That alone is reason for a crowd to show up Saturday when things tip off at 2 p.m. and fans can get their first look at the 2026-27 lineup.

Junior point guard Allie Turner, who has started nearly all Gonzaga games since her arrival from St. Louis, Missouri, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

Turner hopes the Zags put forward a better showing than a year ago.

“Hopefully we’re way better than last year,” Turner said of Fan Fest. “I remember some people being like ‘(we) should have moved (Fan Fest) back a few weeks last year.’ But hopefully this year we look like a well-oiled machine out there.”

GU coach Lisa Fortier was told that Turner brought up Fan Fest and her expectation of making a better debut this year.

“It’s funny that Allie brought up Fan Fest. I don’t even remember it to be honest with you,” Fortier said.

Fortier won’t be looking at the final statistics. She doesn’t put much stock in who scores what or who has the most rebounds in a scrimmage.

“The big thing is getting them under the lights,” Fortier said. “It’s good to see where everyone is. For me it’s good for my coaches to get to coach. I sit on the side and rib everybody and take notes.”

Ten of the 13 Zags have suited up for a Fan Fest. It’ll be a new experience for freshman forward Abby Lusk, GU’s lone incoming frosh from Pocatello, Idaho; guard Emmy Roach, a junior transfer from Rider University; and guard Jocelyn Medina, a senior transfer from Denver.

A roster is usually needed for Fan Fest. Not this year. Even returning is graduate guard Ines Bettencourt, who gained a fifth year of eligibility this summer late under the new 5-in-5 eligibility format. So her former uniform number (8) had been assigned to Medina. Bettencourt’s new number is 0.

Former Mead standout Teryn Gardner, who transferred from Boise State last year and made an immediate impact coming off the bench, is looking forward to Fan Fest.

“We have basically the same team back so I think we’re all super excited for that,” Gardner said. “It’s going to be a fun time.”

Gardner said the goal for Fan Fest isn’t anything complicated.

“We want to start solidifying our plays,” she said. “We want to help the three new girls get to know everything and how we run the system and whatnot. We want to have fun but we want to make it a good scrimmage.”

Sophomore forward Jaiden Haile will be sitting on the sideline. She’s still wearing a boot on a foot she injured during the summer. The injury is healing and doesn’t appear to be longterm, Fortier said.

Haile was selected as the West Coast Conference Sixth Woman of the Year last season.

Fortier has been cautious with Haile’s recovery.

A deep roster

It stands to figure Gonzaga will be a much more polished team this year.

But there are questions to be answered. Can GU win a championship in the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12? Can it win an NCAA Tournament game and go further than any previous GU team? With all five starters back, does coach Fortier just roll out the 2025-26 starting lineup? And with five other returners who got quality playing time, how does Fortier divvy up minutes?

Lots of questions and no hurry to come up with answers.

It shouldn’t come as a surprise that Fortier has decided to stay away from concrete specified goals with her team this year.

“We’re not even really setting those in the same way,” Fortier said. “Our team goal is to show up every day in practice. We’re not even putting that (goals) to paper. We talk about the process a lot. I think it does them a disservice to (talk about goals). They may or may not have those in the back of their heads, but we’re not gonna verbalize those things. I believe if we show up every day and try to get better then all of the end is going to take care of itself.”

Fortier is right. There will be much conversation about potential by a number of people – right, wrong or indifferent – so the Zags would do themselves favors by veering away from those conversations.

They know, for example, they’ll have a target on their backs. With essentially the whole team back they can’t help but be picked to win the Pac-12 Conference and advance to the NCAA Tournament.

There will also be talk of the potential to be the best team ever under Fortier and best in school history. But it does the Zags no good to get caught up in those expectations.

Gonzaga is going to be good. The Zags know it. The Bulldogs will be out to stack days together. And that could get them to where they want to go.

Gonzaga.title: Experienced Gonzaga women return Ines Bettencourt after court ruling: 'It's a new energy'
Gonzaga.summary:
Expectations are going to be high for the Gonzaga women’s basketball team in 2026-27.

A late addition to the roster now may blow those expectations through the roof of McCarthey Athletic Center.

The Zags were set to essentially return their entire team from 2025-26 with the exception of guard Ines Bettencourt, who graduated last spring.

The NCAA’s new five-years-to-play-five-seasons eligibility model announced this summer opened the door for the Portugal native to fight for an additional year of eligibility. She joined a California class action lawsuit, gaining a temporary restraining order and immediate eligibility.

Bettencourt returned to Spokane on Sept. 5.

Now the band is back together for Gonzaga, which will have one of the deepest rosters in the nation with 10 returners, including five starters to go with two transfers and one freshman.

Bettencourt and GU coach Lisa Fortier were cautious in calling it a done deal when the Zags took the court for their first preseason practice last week. A preliminary hearing on Tuesday in Santa Clara County appeared to push a final decision to October 20, at the earliest. 

The Zags are proceeding as if they’ll have Bettencourt.

“It’s been a long summer ever since I graduated,” said Bettencourt, who went back to Portugal and practiced frequently with her national team. “I kind of knew that this would be a possibility. So I was just working behind the scenes and talking with Lisa (Fortier), not really telling anyone else because it wasn’t for sure.”

As soon as the NCAA adopted the new eligibility format, Bettencourt began talking to Fortier and Gonzaga compliance officials “to figure out what exactly I have to do to come back because as an international it’s harder to come back than an American.”

There Bettencourt was going through drills and running up and down the court with her teammates like she had never left.

“Like McKynnlie (Dalan, senior forward) said, ‘we set you off, (had) all these goodbyes and now you’re back.’ ”

Fortier said Gonzaga will proceed as if Bettencourt will be eligible the whole season.

“She had asked us pretty early on in April or May (about coming back) and she was kind of joking at first,” Fortier said. “No one actually thought that any of this was gonna happen. The answer was like sure (you can come back).”

Bettencourt is stoked to have another year with her coaches and what she calls her “best friends.”

“Just having one more shot at this, making the (NCAA) Tournament. Just being more prepared for whatever’s next for me,” Bettencourt said. “So it’s just awesome. Everyone was happy for me.”

Fortier is overjoyed to have Bettencourt back – something the Zags never thought would be an option four months ago.

“She’s one of ours so we would love to have her back,” Fortier said. “She shows up every day around the program and she takes care of business like a professional. She’s a pro in all ways.”

The familiarity will be a team strength no doubt.

“We know each other,” Bettencourt said. “So it was just super nice for them to receive me well again.”

Bettencourt spent most of the summer playing 3-on-3 in Portugal. It was different preparation for returning to Gonzaga.

“I have to run more now,” Bettencourt said, smiling.

Bettencourt took over a leadership role last year as the team’s lone senior. Now as a graduate, she wants to continue to lean into leadership.

“Just building on the leadership,” she said.

She expects to be a better player, too.

“Stay composed and stay consistent at everything,” she said about her personal expectations. “I’m just taking it day by day because I get to come back and be with my teammates, with my coaches, and practice with them again.”

Junior point guard Allie Turner started alongside Bettencourt in the backcourt last year. Turner, Bettencourt and sophomore forward Lauren Whittaker all lived together last year.

The trio can’t run that arrangement back as living assignments had already been passed out. But Turner is glad to have Bettencourt along for one more year.

“We’re super happy to have her back,” Turner said. “It’s a new energy.”

Whittaker agreed.

“For a long time we didn’t really think it was an option. And then kind of a quick turnaround within a couple of weeks we heard (she) was coming back,” Whittaker said. “She’s a player that I think is really seamless to bring back to the team. She has a lot of experience and was a great leader last year and obviously a great player. So it was kind of just an easy transition for her and everyone has been really supportive of it. It’s kind of like she’s never left.”

Bettencourt is looking forward to returning to McCarthey Athletic Center and seeing the fans for FanFest on Oct. 10.

“Super excited,” Bettencourt said. “I’m sure they (the fans) are going to be like ‘what? What are you doing here again?’ But I’m super excited to be back in front of all the fans with my team and showing them again what we can bring this year.”

For a good chunk of this week's episode of State of the Beavs, we're looking at that decision and what it means for the overall growth of the program - even if JaMarcus Shephard would rather take things one game at a time. 

You'll hear clips both from Shephard's media availability coming out of the bye week, and from Legree's announcement at his high school in Baltimore before we look at the Beavers' matchup with Fresno State in California on Halloween. 

With just a few days before the start of college basketball season, it's also time to look at the Beaver men's and women's programs. John Severs and Ben Pahl were present at Oregon State's media day in Portland last week and join the show to offer their perspectives.

All that, plus the five college football games that you need to watch over Halloween weekend. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Questions Following Oregon State Football's 5-2 Start To 2026
Oregon State.summary:
Oregon State are one win away from reaching bowl eligibility in JaMarcus Shephard's first season as head coach after a 48-30 victory against the Washington State Cougars. Of course, we dive into a recap of the action from that contest as Jesse Legree, AJ Newberry, and the rest of the Beavers continue to spearhead a monumental turnaround. Hear audio from Takari Hickle and Trey Glasper about that result.

However, it's also important to note that after the contest, Shephard was quick to offer condolences to the families of the victims of last weeks' tragic shooting in Bend at Silver Rail Elementary.  Hear Shephard's comments, and why they matter to the state and the college football community at-large.

After that, your host Matt Bagley dives into three questions that have arisen in our minds about the Beavers' season following the hot start.

All that, and the five college football games you should watch this week as the Beavers get a bye week to prepare for a road matchup with Fresno State to close the month of October. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Jesse Legree Continues To Set Records For Oregon State Football
Oregon State.summary:
En route to a 4-2 record for Oregon State football, true freshman wide receiver Jesse Legree has been one of the most electrifying players in the country.  The Baltimore native became the first Oregon State wide receiver ever to post over 100 receiving yards in six consecutive games, something not even legendary Beavers like Brandin Cooks and Mike Hass were able to do back in their day.

This week on State of the Beavs, we react to the incredible pace that Legree has set for himself while leading the nation in both receiving yards and touchdowns. We'll also react to Oregon State's thorough beatdown of San Diego State by a score of 66-14 this past weekend, which has made fans realize JaMarcus Shephard's talk of chasing a Pac-12 title is more than simply talk.

Ahead of the Oregon State-Washington State contest this week, we'll predict how things might go against Kirby Moore's squad, and look forward to the reunion with former Beavs head coach Trent Bray.

All that, plus the five games that you need to watch in college football this weekend. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football Looks To Sustain Momentum Against San Diego State
Oregon State.summary:
To start their first conference schedule in the relaunched Pac-12, the Oregon State Beavers picked up a blowout win over Colorado State this past weekend. Braden Atkinson and Jesse Legree continued their impressive run of form and the tight ends also got heavily involved en route to the 56-26 result. Time to review that result and what else worked for JaMarcus Shephard to get his team to a 3-2 record on the year.

This Saturday, the Beavers host a 2-3 San Diego State squad, who are coming off of a dramatic 31-29 win over the Texas State Bobcats. What challenges does Sean Lewis' team present to the Beavers as the Aztecs deal with a mumps outbreak? In addition to our thoughts, you'll hear clips from Shephard's media availability, as well as offensive coordinator Mitch Dahlen and defensive coordinator Mike MacIntyre.

All that, plus a look at the five college football games that Matt Bagley thinks you should watch this weekend. 

Thank you for your support of the show, and as always, Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Oregon State Football Returns to a Pac-12 Schedule
Oregon State.summary:
After a win over the UTEP Miners in El Paso, the Oregon State Beavers are 2-2 under the direction of JaMarcus Shephard. While many Power Conference programs around the nation likely wouldn't be satisfied with that type of start, it's important to keep perspective on the progress made in Shephard's first several months leading the team. 

As your host Matt Bagley looks at that, you'll also hear audio from JaMarcus Shephard's Monday press conference. Oregon State travels to Fort Collins this week for their Pac-12 opener against the Colorado State Rams. 

In between all the football talk, we also take some time to discuss the No. 21 Oregon State men's soccer team with our own John Severs, as they get into the home stretch of the 2026 season.

All that, and a look at the five games that you should watch during your college football weekend. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: Beaver Football Looks To Sustain Momentum After First Win of Shephard Era
Oregon State.summary:
Oregon State football have their first win under JaMarcus Shephard's direction after defeating the Montana Grizzlies this past Saturday by a score of 52-17. 

After that contest, Shephard praised his team's efforts to get their first victory on the board and take heed of the message he has been trying to send since he arrived in Corvallis: that this is only the beginning. This week, you'll hear part of the audio from Shephard's Monday presser and his thoughts on this week's return trip to Texas to face the UTEP Miners in El Paso.

On this week's State of the Beavs, your host Matt Bagley also dives into what we, as a fanbase, learned about this Beaver team from the Montana game and what the next steps should be in order to sustain that momentum moving forward.

All that, plus Bagley's five games to watch in college football this weekend as conference play begins in most of the country. Go Beavs.

Cougars Narrowly Fall To San Diego State 26-20
WSU football falls short vs. San Diego State, loses 6th straight
Washington State.summary: In what’s been an all too familiar feeling for WSU football this season, the Cougars fell short of a comeback, losing to San Diego State, their sixth straight.
Washington State.author: Greg Woods

Washington State.title: 5 thoughts from WSU's loss to San Diego State | Rewind
Washington State.summary:
SAN DIEGO – At some point in the fourth quarter, not long after Washington State angled toward mounting a comeback against San Diego State in Saturday’s game, things began to feel a bit eerie.

Driving down the field, the Cougars were facing a 26-14 deficit. Moments later, quarterback Owen Eshelman pulled a read option and jogged untouched into the end zone, letting out a good scream as he did so. All of a sudden, as listless as this WSU effort felt only a few moments prior, the visitors were angling toward a comeback.

It conjured memories of a certain game from two years ago: In 2024, in a road game against San Diego State, the Cougars were looking at a 26-14 hole in the fourth quarter. They made up the ground in the fourth quarter, sandwiching two John Mateer touchdowns around a Buddah Al-Uqdah interception, a string of winning plays to pull off a stunning rally.

These Cougars had no such luck Saturday night. Their final drive petered out around midfield, where right tackle Jaylin Caldwell was called for a false start, coach Kirby Moore took his final timeout to prevent the ensuing 10-second runoff and Eshelman’s final two passes fell incomplete, handing the ball back to the Aztecs.

With six straight loss es, WSU (1-8, 0-5 Pac-12) has three games left to find its first FBS win of the season. The Cougars are idle next week, giving them a chance to rest for the first time after nine games.

Here are five thoughts from the game.

1. WSU has to generate more sacks

After nine games, the Cougars have generated only eight sacks, which ranks No. 134 of 138 FBS teams. That’s not exactly what Moore had in mind when he landed transfers Matyus McLain and Linus Zunk out of the transfer portal last winter. WSU did not produce any sacks in Saturday’s game, the second straight sack-less game the team has played.

This season, McLain and Zunk have had few issues creating havoc in backfields, but the sacks have eluded them. On Saturday, they largely struck out on both fronts. WSU engineered only six pressures on SDSU redshirt freshman quarterback Stone Saunders, according to Pro Football Focus, including two from McLain and one from Zunk.

Simply put: The Cougars have to get more pressure on quarterbacks, and they have to bring them down when they have the chance. On one play in Saturday’s game, cornerback Khamari Terrell had Saunders wrapped up for what looked like an easy sack, but Saunders wiggled free.

2. It’s probably time to abandon the run game altogether

WSU running backs Kirby Vorhees, Maxwell Woods and Leo Pulalasi combined for only 34 yards on 14 carries, an average rush of 2.4 yards. Here is how they have fared in eight FBS games this season.

• Washington: 16 carries, 38 yards.

• Kansas State: 17 carries, 72 yards.

• Arizona: 17 carries, 59 yards.

• Fresno State: 12 carries, 45 yards.

• Utah State: 19 carries, 77 yards.

• Oregon State: 13 carries, 26 yards.

• Boise State: 10 carries, 20 yards.

• SDSU: 14 carries, 34 yards.

That comes out to an average of 15 carries for 46 yards, some of the worst numbers in the country. It’s clear the problem comes in large part from the Cougars’ offensive line, which can’t move bodies in short-yardage situations. Maybe that group can solve some things for its final three games of the season, but it’s more likely that WSU can find success by doing away with the running game for the most part.

3. Cougars’ perimeter tackling left a lot to be desired

WSU’s last two opponents, Boise State and San Diego State, were wise to realize something: They couldn’t generate many yards up the middle, where Cougar defensive linemen have done well to bottle things up, but they could very easily bounce to the outside and jet upfield.

That’s how SDSU running back Javion Kinnard scored both of his touchdowns, making WSU defenders like nickelback Jamarey Smith and Jeremiah Bernard miss on his way to the end zone. The Cougars missed 10 tackles in this one, according to PFF, which is better than the 16 they missed against Boise State.

But when you aren’t getting sacks and aren’t generating many turnovers – even with safety Jaylen Thomas’ interception, his third of the year, the Cougs have forced only six turnovers, which is tied for No. 121 nationally – you have to tackle well. WSU has not done so recently.

4. WSU’s offense sustained drives well, but finishing remains elusive

The Cougs converted 9 of 14 third downs in Saturday’s game, an encouraging development to one of the team’s biggest weaknesses all year, which allowed them to sustain several drives. They scored one touchdown on a drive that chewed up nearly five minutes and covered 75 yards, then another on a series that elapsed 6 minutes , 15 seconds and went 64 yards. WSU converted 5 of its first 6 third downs, including two on Eshelman keepers.

But the Cougs couldn’t always finish their long drives. In the third frame, they used up 6:25 to march 40 yards in 13 plays, but on a third-and-10, Eshelman showed his inexperience by committing a costly intentional grounding penalty, resulting in a loss of 14 yards.

That set up a fourth-and-long from the 35, which meant a 53-yard field goal try for kicker Jack Stevens. His attempt went wide left and well short, scuttled by the rainy and windy conditions.

The Cougs also missed a chance to capitalize on Thomas’ interception, which landed their offense at the Aztecs 36. They ran three plays, got to fourth down and couldn’t convert.

5. The bye comes at a good time for WSU

Every coach in America will say the same thing about their team’s bye week: It comes at a good time. But it’s especially true for these Cougars, who will get an extra week to prepare for a home game against Colorado State, which harbors the worst defense in college football.

Theoretically, WSU shouldn’t need much help taking down such a lowly defense, but the Cougars also managed 20 points against an SDSU defense that had given up point totals of 41, 66 and 56. With a week off, look for Moore and the Cougs to make the adjustments they need to earn their first FBS win of the year.

Washington State.title: Dan Doornink, WSU hall of famer and longtime Seahawks running back, dies at 70
Washington State.summary:
Dan Doornink, a standout running back at Wapato High and Washington State University who then went on to an eight-year NFL career that included seven seasons with the Seahawks, has died at the age of 70, the Seahawks announced Sunday.

Doornink gained 1,836 yards with 15 touchdowns in 105 games for Seattle and may be best remembered for gaining 123 yards in a 13-7 wild-card playoff win over the defending Super Bowl champion Los Angeles Raiders at the Kingdome in 1984.

Doornink was affectionately known as “Dr. Dan” or simply “Dr.” for studying at the UW Medical School while playing for the Seahawks.

“I was competing against guys who didn’t have to study all the time,” Doornink once said in an interview with the Times. “It was hard and challenging and I didn’t get much sleep those years.”

After his NFL career ended he earned a Doctor of Medicine degree at UW and went on to a long career practicing internal medicine in Yakima.

Doornink revealed in 2021 that he had endured a long battle with COVID-19 that was made more difficult by a rare blood disorder. He said in an interview that year with the Seattle Times that he was in intensive care for 23 days and lost 38 pounds.

The team’s statement called Doornink “a beloved member of the Seahawks early days, both on and off the field.”

After a standout career at Wapato High, where the field is now named after him, Doornink recalled in a 2018 interview with the Seattle Times that he signed with WSU and then-coach Jim Sweeney as a quarterback. However, he was far down on the depth chart and moved to running back when injuries hit that position.

He led the Cougars in rushing in both 1976 and 1977, the latter season when WSU opened the season with one of the team’s biggest non-conference road wins ever, a 19-10 victory over 15th-ranked Nebraska. Doornink, a member of WSU’s Hall of Fame, remains 14th on the school’s all-time rushing list with 1,739 yards and is also 25th in career receptions with 105.

Taken 174th overall by the Giants in 1978, he rushed for 306 yards as a rookie despite missing six games with a shoulder injury before being traded to the Seahawks shortly before the start of the 1979 season for a 1980 seventh-round pick.

Doornink became a regular starter for the 1979 and 1980 seasons and then a key rotational player in the backfield from 1981-85. His 1,530 yards with the Seahawks is 14th in franchise history which included a career-high 500 in 1979 when Seattle finished 9-7.

He turned in his career regular season single-game high that season with 122 on 21 carries when the Seahawks beat Atlanta on what was the team’s first-ever appearance on Monday Night Football, a game many remember for Jim Zorn throwing a pass for a first down on a fake field goal to kicker Efren Herrera. That was the only 100-yard game of Doornink’s career in the regular season.

However, he would memorably top that number when Seahawks coach Chuck Knox decided to feature him as part of what was something of a surprise offensive attack emphasizing the running game when the Seahawks hosted the Raiders in the wild card round following the 1984 season. Seattle had lost its final two games against the Chiefs and Broncos, the latter contest costing the Seahawks the AFC West title, due in part to committing nine turnovers combined in the two defeats, including eight interceptions.

Knox decided to get back to basics against the Raiders, unveiling a double tight-end formation that the team used almost exclusively, and Seattle ran it 51 times while throwing just 10 in defeating LA. Doornink, who hadn’t had a carry in the previous two games, got handed the ball a career-high 29 times as the Seahawks took a 13-0 lead and held on.

“They knew exactly what we were going to do and still we were able to get th yards,” a happy Doornink said afterward.

Washington State.title: WSU hoops ready to kick off new season with home matchup against Davidson
Washington State.summary:
Earlier this summer, when David Riley was enjoying a break from coaching the Washington State’s men’s basketball team, he got a ribbing from his brother.

Noah Riley, a quality control coach and analyst for the NFL’s New York Giants, gave him a hard time: Riley teams are so soft.

Back then, Noah was likely referring to the two problems that have plagued Riley’s first two WSU teams: Turnovers and defense. The Cougars finished last season ranked No. 292 in turnover rate and No. 248 in effective field goal percentage defense, painting a picture of an undisciplined, mistake-prone club.

Ahead of Riley’s third season at WSU, which begins with a home matchup against Davidson at 6 p.m. Monday, can the Cougars reverse those trends?

“Well, I think it starts in practice,” said Riley, whose team plays just five home nonconference games this season. “With our teams in the past that have won championships and won a lot of games, there’s been chippy practices, and it’s uncomfortable. And you walk away from practice with just a little bit of uncomfortableness because someone had to lose. I think that’s something that we’ve taken away this year.”

In the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12, WSU will use a retooled roster with 14 newcomers to try and turn around the problems that afflicted the last two Cougar teams. As they head into Monday’s season opener, they’ll likely start the same group that fueled their team’s second and final exhibition game, a road win over rival Washington last week.

That will likely mean lots of touches for East Texas A&M transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, who tallied a team-best 23 points and 11 rebounds in that game, plus opportunities for Central Missouri transfer guard Lazerek Houston and Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips, each of whom scored in double figures. The rest of the Cougs’ starting lineup figures to include UNLV transfer big man Ladji Dembele and Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, whose size could make a difference for a WSU team that has struggled to rebound the past two seasons.

Against Davidson, which was picked to finish eighth of 14 teams in the Atlantic 10 preseason poll, WSU will likely need some more of that recipe. The Cougars played an ugly game to beat the Huskies . The game featured a combined 87 free throws, and neither team shot better than 40% from the field . But they did make nine 3-pointers. They got five combined from Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell and former Eastern Washington wing Casey Jones, who spent the last two years on a church mission.

From a 30,000-foot view, that’s the main contingent that the Cougars will use to replace several key offseason losses, including several to the transfer portal: Ace Glass (Vanderbilt), forward ND Okafor (Mississippi State) and wing Ri Vavers (Memphis), plus guards Jerone Morton (Kentucky) and Tomas Thrastarson (Seattle U), forward Eemeli Yalaho (NC State) and key reserve Parker Gerrits (Wyoming).

This WSU team features only two returners, forward Dominik Robinson and walk-on guard Dio Blakely, which means most of the minutes will belong to transfers. A few other names to watch include TCU transfer RJ Jones and French freshman forward Mohamed Sankhe.

Sankhe totaled five points and three rebounds in 15 minutes against UW.

Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins also figures to make a splash, but because an injury sidelined him for both exhibition games, it’s unclear when he’ll be able to get on the court.

“We’ve got a lot of new faces, and so it’s been a really busy preseason for us trying to get in some concepts,” Riley said. “I think we simplified a few things to make sure that we’re able to play together and play hard, and I think that’s something that just takes time. And I think we’re learning those lessons.”
